### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Running MTP speculative decoding on the OpenVINO backend fails in every configuration I tried. Plain decode (same build, same model, no -md) works fine.

GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=GPU llama-cli -m gemma-4-12b-it.gguf
-md gemma-4-12b-mtp-q8.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp
-ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on -c 4096 -n 128 --temp 0 -p "test prompt"

What I tried:

1. Target and draft both on OpenVINO (command above): crashes during graph compute with a MatMul shape error, then dumps core. See first log block. Looks like the draft graph's raw hidden-state input (3840-dim, fed from the target) doesn't get a dynamic token dimension, so the post-concat MatMul shape-infers wrong.
2. Draft on CPU (-ngld 0): runs and produces correct-looking output, but logs ~505 graph-compute failures over a 128-token generation and decodes at 6.1 t/s — slower than plain decode (8.1 t/s), so speculation makes things worse.
3. Target on OPENVINO0, draft on Vulkan0 (build with both backends): aborts at ggml-backend.cpp:898 (second log block). The Gemma-4 MTP head reads the target's KV cache, which is pre-allocated in the OpenVINO buffer and can't be used from Vulkan.
4. Same as 3 with GGML_OPENVINO_STATEFUL_EXECUTION=1: throws ov::Exception from graph_rewrite.cpp:298 during compile.

This matters: on this iGPU the OpenVINO backend prefills ~6.5x faster than Vulkan (917 vs 142 t/s, pp512, Gemma-4-12B Q4_0), but Vulkan+MTP decodes ~3x faster than OpenVINO (23.5 vs 8.1 t/s). Spec-decode support is the only thing preventing the OpenVINO backend from being strictly better on Intel iGPUs.

## Summary

Under parallel mixed load (`-np 4 --kv-unified`), `llama-server` on an **integrated HIP GPU** (Strix Halo / gfx1151, 128 GB UMA) returns **complete responses that verbatim belong to a different, earlier request**. A large-prompt request receives, as its entire response, the literal answer text of a short request from an earlier round. We also observed a **chimeric** response fusing tokens of two different requests' expected outputs.

**Bisected to a single commit: c7d87229 "ggml-cuda : restore prop.integrated on HIP builds" (#24233).**

| build | result (validated responses, nonce-checked) |
|---|---|
| 505b1ed1 (parent window start) | clean — 0 violations / 168 |
| 5839ba35 (= parent of c7d87229) | clean — 0 / 36 |
| **c7d87229** | **cross-request replays: 3 hard / 36** |
| e8f19cc0 (window end) | cross-request replays: 7 hard + 1 chimera / 96 |

The same harness against **CPU builds** of both window endpoints shows no build-dependent difference (model-compliance noise only) — consistent with the culprit being the HIP integrated-memory path. This presumably explains why it went unnoticed: discrete GPUs are unaffected; it needs an **integrated** AMD GPU (`prop.integrated == 1`), multiple slots and concurrent mixed traffic.

## Environment

- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), gfx1151, 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.14, Ubuntu 24.04
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++` (Release)
- Server: `llama-server -m <model> -ngl 999 -c 65536 -np 4 --kv-unified --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'`
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4-class quant). First hit this in production behind LocalAI (same symptom after its vendored-llama.cpp bump crossed this commit); reproducing on vanilla `llama-server` rules the wrapper out.

## Reproduction

Load pattern per round (~30 s, script below): (B) short "repeat exactly this code: <nonce>" request → (C) large-prompt (~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce in the first line → (D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain). Every response is validated to contain its **own** nonce and no nonce of an **earlier** request.

On affected builds the round-N large-prompt request receives a literal foreign nonce as its complete response, typically from a round-(N−1) burst request. Verbatim from run logs at e8f19cc0:

```
R4/C got='pd-20260722-115649-3-d1'      (expected: reply echoing pc-...-4-c + a summary)
R5/C got='pd-20260722-115649-4-d2'
R6/C got='pd-20260722-115649-1-d1'
R7/C got='pd-20260722-115649-6-d1'
R8/C got='pd-20260722-115649-7-d1'
R3/C got='<!-- run:pc-20260722-115649-2-d0 -->'   <-- chimera: pc-...-2 stem fused with a -d0 burst suffix
```

In production we additionally observed: a poisoned slot re-serving its stored answer to unrelated requests **20+ minutes later** (the victim's `usage` then reports the foreign request's token counts), and occasional degeneration into repeated single characters (`/////...`).

<details><summary>repro-crossover.py (needs httpx)</summary>

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

This PR adds support for MTP (Multi Token Prediction) heads. I tested this on Qwen3.6 27B and Qwen3.6 35BA3B but in principle it should work for any MTP model. I've posted the detailed results below, but typically I see a steady-state acceptance of around 75% with 3 draft tokens, which is more than >2x speed-up over baseline. The design decisions I took to get to this stage are as follows:

- The MTP model is a separate model which loads from the same GGUF, the idea is that MTP should automatically start and we shouldn't need to distribute the MTP gguf separately but also it has it's own context/kv-cache etc. 
- I saw a problem in #18039 where the hidden features weren't propagated correctly across multiple ubatches, so this PR adds a separate "hook" for the MTP to consume after each `ubatch`
- The MTP speculative class is fairly trivial (although it does depend on #22400, but could work without it)

> [!TIP]
> MTP is compatible with Vision input and Tensor/Pipeline Parallelism

> [!NOTE]
> Prompt processing (PP) speed typically takes a negative hit when MTP is enabled mainly due to Device-To-Host (D2H) embedding transfers. It's something to be optimized in the future.

> [!NOTE]
> Parallel decoding with MTP is supported, but not fully optimized yet.

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes a regression after #24233, which restored HIP integrated GPU detection. On my AMD APU, this also made the ROCm host-buffer path available for HIP integrated GPUs. With that path enabled, prompt input appears corrupted: chat templates and system prompts can be ignored, and generated output becomes garbage.

This change keeps integrated GPU detection/reporting intact, but disables direct ROCm_Host compute on HIP integrated GPUs. The fix does not disable host-buffer exposure entirely, pinned buffers remain available to preserve functionality, while only the problematic direct compute path is blocked.

## Additional information

Tested locally on gfx1151 / RDNA3.5 APU with ROCm 7.14. The corrupted input/output issue is fixed with this patch.
The issue appeared in external harnesses like Pi and OpenCode. It can also be reproduced in the built-in web UI with a sufficiently large combined first input. For example, gemma-4-26B-A4B with 4676 tokens of context or more outputs `<unused49>` indefinitely. Other models can be way more resilient and their output starts by saying 'Based on the text provided, which appears to be a corrupted or "hallucinated" version of a Wikipedia article'.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistance to review and patch the relevant code. I tested and reviewed the final change myself.

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-cli --version
version: 9721 (dfsg)
built with gcc for x86_64-linux-gnu
```

(Ubuntu 26.10 `llama.cpp 9721+dfsg-1ubuntu1` package, `libggml0-backend-hip 0.15.2-1` from the `ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics` PPA, ROCm 7.2.4.)

I have also confirmed the underlying pattern still exists on `master` (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` — host `get_device_table_id(int cc)` at ~line 89 and device `get_device_table_id()` at ~line 73 use two different lookups). See "Why #24129 doesn't fully close this" below.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 w/ Radeon 860M (gfx1152, RDNA3.5, Strix Halo family iGPU), integrated 16 GiB VRAM (UMA).

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0` (any Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/Q6_K/IQ4_NL model that dispatches through the MMVQ `n=1` path reproduces).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

MMVQ produces `NaN` outputs for `ncols_dst == 1` (batch=1 decode) whenever the loaded HIP code object was compiled for `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` and the runtime device is RDNA3.5 (gfx1150/gfx1152/gfx1153 without native code in the fatbin). Symptom in `llama-cli` is coherent-looking prompt processing followed by tokens rendered as `?????...` at plausible generation rates. HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0 (native gfx1100) or =11.5.1 (native gfx1151) both hide the bug — they steer HIP to a native code object instead of `gfx11-generic`.

**Minimal repro** (fatbin without a gfx1152 native code object; equivalent to the current Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build):

```
lxc launch --ephemeral --profile rocm-gpu ubuntu-daily:stonking generics-repro
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo add-apt-repository ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics -y
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo apt install -y llama.cpp libggml0-backend-hip

# NaN outputs from MMVQ (all n=1 cases fail):
lxc exec generics-repro -- /usr/libexec/x86_64-linux-gnu/ggml/test-backend-ops test -b ROCm0 -o MUL_MAT -p 'type_a=q4_0'
# ...
# [MUL_MAT] NaN at index 0 (ROCm0=nan CPU=4.080024)   MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0,type_b=f32,m=16,n=1,k=256,...): FAIL
# every n=1 case fails; every n>=2 case passes

# Garbage tokens from llama-cli:
lxc exec generics-repro -- bash -c "echo 'What is 2+2?' | llama-cli -hf unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0 --predict 15 --single-turn"
# > What is 2+2?
# | ???????????????
```

`AMD_LOG_LEVEL=3` on the failing run shows the runtime resolving to the generic code object:

```
Using generic code object for device: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx1152 co: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx11-generic
```

### Root cause

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` has two `get_device_table_id()`s and they disagree on `gfx11-generic` + RDNA3.5:

- **Device** (`__device__`, ~line 73), compile-time preprocessor: for `gfx11-generic`, `__GFX11__` is set (so `RDNA3` is defined) but none of `__gfx1150/51/52/53__` are set (so `RDNA3_5` stays undefined) → `RDNA3_0` is defined → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA3_0`. For Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL at `ncols_dst == 1`, `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 8 (2 for Q6_K). The kernel is emitted with `__launch_bounds__(8*warp_size, 1)` and sizes `__shared__ float tmp_shared[nwarps-1][...][warp_size]` for an 8-way inter-warp reduction.
- **Host** (`__host__`, ~line 89), runtime `cc`: on gfx1152 `cc = GGML_CUDA_CC_OFFSET_AMD + 0x1152`, so `GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA3_5(cc)` is true → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2` → `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 1 → launches `block_dims = (warp_size, 1, 1)`.

Only warp 0 executes, so the `if (threadIdx.y > 0) tmp_shared[threadIdx.y-1][...] = ...` writes never happen. The reduction loop `for (int l = 0; l < nwarps-1; ++l) tmp[j][i] += tmp_shared[l][...];` runs with `nwarps == 8` (compile-time), reading uninitialized LDS for `l = 0..6` → NaN, then propagates through the rest of the graph and shows up as `?????` at the sampler.

Confirmed by the test-backend-ops bisection: every `MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0, n=1, ...)` case fails with `NaN at index 0`; every `n>=2` case passes. That's exactly the `if (ncols_dst == 1)` boundary in `calc_nwarps` where the RDNA3_0 branch would return 8 vs. falling through to 1.

Trivial FP32 kernels compiled the same way (`--offload-arch=gfx11-generic`) and run on the same gfx1152 produce correct results, so this is not a general clang miscompile of the generic target — it's specifically a host/device disagreement on the MMVQ tuning table.

### Why PR #24129 doesn't fully close this

[#24129](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24129) (merged) added `__gfx1152__` / `__gfx1153__` to the `RDNA3_5` macro in `hip.h`. That is the right fix for the case where the fatbin **does** ship a native gfx1152 code object — the runtime loads native gfx1152, the device compile sees `__gfx1152__` → `RDNA3_5` → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2`, matches the host. Great.

But if a build has `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` in its target list without a native gfx1152, the runtime falls through to the generic code object, and `__gfx11_generic__` (which *is* set for the generic target — confirmed with `hipcc --offload-arch=gfx11-generic -E -dM`) is not part of the `RDNA3_5` macro. So on that same hardware the mismatch is unchanged. This is the situation in the Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build (whose target list, via `rocm-target-arch` from `pkg-rocm-tools`, currently emits `gfx11-generic gfx1100 gfx1101 gfx1151 …` without gfx1152/1153) and, from what I can tell, in the TheRock build path that [#25436](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/25436) (DeepSeek V4 garbled on Strix Halo, still open) and possibly [#24962](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24962) are hitting.

More generally, the host/device pattern is inherently fragile: any future target/generic pair where the two lookups disagree will silently reintroduce this. The specific instance was fixed but the root shape wasn't.

### Proposed fix

Derive `nwarps` from the compiled kernel instead of recomputing it on the host: refactor `calc_launch_params` to be templat

## Bug: AMD GPU token substitution corruption on Qwen3.6-27B (both Vulkan and ROCm)

### Summary

All models produce consistent character substitution errors in generated text on AMD GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm). The CPU backend produces correct output. Cloud vLLM with the same model also produces correct output. The corruption is deterministic, reproducible, and not model-specific.

**Version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)

### Symptom

URLs and long token sequences get corrupted with character substitutions. Examples from Qwen3.6-27B:

| Input | GPU output |
|-------|-----------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zh-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zshell-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-ssh-plugins` |
| `froggeric` | `frogger` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix-Assist` |

Short strings like `zsh-plugins` reproduce correctly in isolation. The corruption only appears in longer sequences, suggesting precision accumulation in attention over longer contexts.

### Reproduction

1. Start llama-server with any GGUF model on AMD GPU (Vulkan or ROCm backend)
2. Send a chat completion asking to repeat a URL:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "code",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise assistant. Repeat exactly."},
      {"role": "user", "content": "Repeat this URL exactly:\nhttps://github.com/unixorn/awesome-zsh-plugins/blob/main/README.md"}
    ],
    "max_tokens": 100,
    "temperature": 0.0
  }'
```

3. Observe corrupted URL in the response
4. Run the same request on CPU backend (`--n-gpu-layers 0`) and observe correct output

### Environment

- **GPU 0:** AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (Navi 31, RDNA3, discrete)
- **GPU 1:** AMD Ryzen 9 9950X integrated GPU (RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO)
- **Vulkan driver:** Mesa RADV 26.1.6, Vulkan API 1.4.354
- **ROCm:** latest (via `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`)
- **Kernel:** 6.17.9
- **llama.cpp version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)
- **Containers:** `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-vulkan` and `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`

### Exclusion testing

Every variable tested produces identical corruption on GPU. Only the CPU backend is correct.

| Variable | Values tested | Result |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| Model quants | Q4_K_XL, Q4_K_M, UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-Q5_K_XL | All corrupted |
| GPU backend | Vulkan (RADV), ROCm (HIP) | Both corrupted |
| KV cache type | q8_0, f16 | Both corrupted |
| GPU count | Both GPUs, single GPU (`GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0`) | Both corrupted |
| Speculative decoding | On (draft-mtp), off | Both corrupted |
| Thinking/reasoning | Enabled, disabled | Both corrupted |
| Chat template | Custom template, raw completion | Both corrupted |
| Temperature | 0.0 (greedy) | Still corrupted |
| **CPU backend** | `--n-gpu-layers 0` | **Correct** |

Forcing a single GPU via `GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0` rules out multi-GPU issues like #26197.

### Not model-specific: Gemma 4 also corrupts

Tested Gemma 4 31B (`gemma-4-31B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`) on the same Vulkan backend. It also corrupts URLs, but with a different pattern — inserting spaces instead of substituting characters:

| Input | Gemma 4 output |
|-------|---------------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome zsh-plugins` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix assist` |
| `froggeric` | `froggereric` |
| `Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates` | `Qwen-Fixed-Chat- Templates` |

The corruption pattern differs by model (Qwen3.6 substitutes characters, Gemma 4 inserts spaces) but both produce incorrect output on AMD GPU.

### Not a model issue: cloud vLLM is correct

The same Qwen3.6-27B model running on cloud vLLM (different quant, different inference engine) reproduces all test URLs perfectly. This confirms the corruption is specific to llama.cpp on AMD GPU.

### Conclusion

This is a general AMD GPU compute issue in llama.cpp, not model-specific, not quant-specific, not backend-specific. It affects all models on the RX 7900 XTX. Both GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm) produce identical corruption patterns, suggesting a shared AMD code path issue.

Potentially related issues:
- #26197 (multiple AMD GPUs lead to gibberish output) — ruled out by single-GPU test
- #20029 (Vulkan garbage output on AMD)
- #25612 (split-mode garbled output)

### Name and Version

Built from `505b1ed1` (2026-07-15). The relevant code is **unchanged in current master** (`86d86ed`, 2026-07-17): the assert at `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282` and `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` are as described below.

### Operating systems

macOS (Apple Silicon, arm64 / NEON)

### GGML backends

CPU (Metal build, but run with `-ngl 0`)

### Hardware

Apple Silicon, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`bullerwins/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-GGUF` — `DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf` (arch `deepseek4`; attention in Q8_0, routed experts in MXFP4).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On **Apple Silicon (arm64/NEON), CPU only (`-ngl 0`)**, `deepseek4` (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) produces **garbled output** — an endless run of `=` — instead of text. This is **not** the CUDA/ROCm expert issue in #25582 / #25436, and not fixed by the rejected assert change in #25412. It is the **CPU online-repack path silently corrupting `blk.N.attn_output_a` / `blk.N.attn_output_b`** (the MLA low-rank output projection).

```
./llama-cli -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf -ngl 0 -cnv -st -p "What is the capital of France? Answer briefly."
# -> [Start thinking] ==================================================  (garbage)
```

**Bisection** (each variant is a one-line change to `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` returning `nullptr` for the named tensors, then a full rebuild + rerun):

| repack disabled for… | output |
|---|---|
| nothing (stock) | garbled (also hits the `:4282` assert on the 3D expert stacks) |
| 3D tensors only (`ggml_n_dims != 2`) | **still garbled** |
| the DSA `indexer` tensors | still garbled |
| `attn_kv` | still garbled |
| `attn_q_a` / `attn_q_b` | still garbled |
| **`attn_output_a` / `attn_output_b`** | **correct** ("Paris") |
| everything | correct |

So the culprit is exactly `attn_output_a/_b` — 86 of 494 tensors. Excluding *only* those from repack yields coherent output.

**Controls (both pass with fully stock repack on the same machine):**
- `gemma4-31b` Q4_K_M (dense) — correct.
- `Agents-A1` Q8_0 (`qwen35moe`, 256 routed experts) — correct.

So this is **`deepseek4`-specific**, not a general MoE or 3D-tensor repack problem — a 256-expert MoE and a dense model both repack fine.

### Root cause (analysis)

`ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` selects a repack `tensor_traits` purely by tensor **type** (q4_0/q4_K/q5_K/q6_K/q2_K/q8_0/iq4_nl/mxfp4) and `ne[1] % 8`; it **never checks `ggml_n_dims`** and does not exclude the MLA output-projection tensors. `extra_buffer_type::supports_op` *claims* `MUL_MAT_ID` for 3D `src0` (`repack.cpp:4795`), but the compute path `forward_mul_mat` asserts 2D (`repack.cpp:4282`). For `attn_output_a/_b` specifically, repacking reorders the weight in memory and the result read back is wrong — silently, when the assert is avoided.

Note: changing the assert to `>= 2` (as in the rejected #25412) is not a fix — it turns the crash into silent garbage, which is what the "3D tensors only" row above shows.

I'm happy to test a proper patch. The mechanism for why `attn_output_a/_b` in particular is affected (while `attn_q_a/_b`, same type, is not) I have not pinned down — likely how those tensors are consumed in the `deepseek4` MLA graph after repack reorders them.

### Relevant log output

```
/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282: GGML_ASSERT(ggml_n_dims(op->src[0]) == 2) failed
  ...forward_mul_mat_id... (stock repack, before any workaround)
```

items.body: ### Why this exists On AMD, image generation came out visibly wrong at 1024×1024 and larger: a ghosted, doubled subject that got worse as the resolution grew. Smaller resolutions were clean, and the same job ran clean on CPU and on NVIDIA, so it was specific to AMD and only showed above a certain resolution. The flash-attention kernel was quietly ignoring the precision the model asked for and running in half precision instead. That is usually harmless, but at large resolutions the rounding piles up until it shows in the image. Worse, it fails silently: no error, just a wrong, ghosted picture. ### What it does When the model asks for fp32 precision, the kernel now uses it, instead of quietly running in half precision. Where fp32 will not fit, it falls back to the existing path, so those cases stay unchanged. This only affects AMD/HIP. NVIDIA never uses this kernel, so CUDA builds are untouched. ### Why it's the right fix Before this, there was no way to get a correct image out of an affected AMD GPU. The kernel did not fall back to anything; it just silently produced a garbled result. The only way to a correct image was to give up on the GPU and run on the CPU, which is far slower. So this is not a slower-path tradeoff: it makes the AMD GPU usable for these images, where before it was quietly broken. Builds with rocWMMA enabled already had a correct GPU path; this fix is for the AMD setups that do not. ### How I found it I reproduced it with Chroma (a non-GQA model, head size 128) in stable-diffusion.cpp on an RDNA4 GPU (a Radeon AI PRO R9700), built without rocWMMA flash-attention. Comparing the same generation on the CPU and on the GPU step by step, everything matched until the attention step (the `FLASH_ATTN_EXT` op), which was the one place the GPU result diverged. It also does not show up in `test-backend-ops`, because that test's synthetic inputs are too uniform to trigger the rounding. It surfaced alongside a separate bug on the same path, an incorrect mask shape in masked flash attention, which I fixed upstream in [leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp#1625](https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/pull/1625) (merged). Those two changes are independent; together they make Chroma's masked flash attention correct on HIP. ### Validation The clearest way to see the bug is to render the same prompt and seed on several backends and compare. The correct backends agree on one image; the unpatched AMD tile kernel is the lone outlier, and the fix brings it back into agreement. Chroma1-HD, 1280², 20 steps, euler, flash attention on, fixed seed: - **NVIDIA (A100)**, **AMD with matrix cores** (rocWMMA), and **AMD with the fix** (fp32 tile) all produce the same image. - **AMD without the fix** (fp16 tile) produces a different, ghosted, wrong image. That is the point: the unpatched AMD result is not "just a different valid render." Three correct paths converge on one image: a different vendor (NVIDIA) and two different AMD kernels, the matrix-core rocWMMA path and the fp32 tile fix. Only the unpatched fp16 tile diverges. With the fix, that path rejoins them. At higher resolution the unpatched path degrades further, to a fully black image at 2048, while the others stay correct. Environment: - NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB: driver 580.159.04, CUDA 13.0 - AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201): ROCm 7.2.4, amdgpu 6.16.13 `test-backend-ops` is unchanged; head sizes 512 and 576 fall back to fp16. ### Reproduction Reproduced via stable-diffusion.cpp (commit `4e85e07`), which vendors this ggml kernel. Build `sd-cli` for AMD (HIP): ``` cmake -B build -DSD_HIPBLAS=ON -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1201 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build -j --target sd-cli ``` The wrong result is this build as-is (the unpatched fp16 tile path); the correct result is the same build with this PR's ggml patch applied. For the NVIDIA reference, configure with `-DSD_CUDA=ON` instead. Render (identical command on every backend, only the build differs): ``` ./sd-cli -M img_gen \ --diffusion-model Chroma1-HD.safetensors \ --t5xxl t5xxl_fp16.safetensors \ --vae ae.safetensors \ -p "a photograph of a dog on the beach, photorealistic, hyperrealistic, highly detailed, sharp focus, natural lighting, DSLR" \ --cfg-scale 4.0 --guidance 3.5 --sampling-method euler --steps 20 \ -W 1280 -H 1280 --seed 42 --rng cuda --chroma-enable-t5-mask --diffusion-fa \ -o out.png ``` ### Performance note This is the tile flash-attention kernel, the path used whenever the matrix-core path (rocWMMA flash-attention) is not in use. That path is opt-in, a build flag that is off by default, so a default HIP build runs the tile kernel on any AMD GPU, with or without matrix cores. The tile kernel has no hardware-accelerated fp32. On RDNA the fast fp16 path uses a packed dot instruction that fp32 cannot use, and fp32 storage roughly doubles the shared memory the kernel needs, which lowers occupancy. So running this kernel in fp32 is inherently slower than fp16. It is still far faster than the only correct option this path had before, which was to fall back to the CPU. That slowdown is not a reason to leave it broken. The kernel is an active code path, and this is current hardware, not a legacy quirk: it was caught on an RDNA4 Radeon AI PRO R9700. Any build without rocWMMA flash-attention lands here, and the hardware affected worst is anything with no matrix cores at all, such as the RDNA2 generation, which cannot use rocWMMA and so has the tile kernel as its only attention path, with no faster option to switch to. All of them silently produce a ghosted image. GPUs that do have the matrix-core path keep using it and are unaffected. For everyone on the fallback, a small and correct slowdown is far better than a fast and wrong result.

items.body:
This patch fixes 4 distinct bugs in ggml-backend.cpp that cause garbled/Chinese output when using --n-cpu-moe with long prompts (>1000 tokens).

## Bugs Fixed

1. **Copy slot exhaustion**: The circular buffer next_copy wraps and reuses stale expert weights during decode when multiple copy slots exist. Fix: reset next_copy on every sync when n_copies > 1.

2. **Bitset OOB**: Expert ID scan loop can read past n_expert when no experts are assigned to a split. Fix: add id < n_expert guard after the while loop.

3. **Cross-split staleness**: prev_ids_tensor was hoisted outside the split loop, causing stale tensor comparisons across splits. Fix: move declaration inside the split loop.

4. **Async barrier missing**: graph_compute_async was called without ensuring async copies complete for backends without cpy_tensor_async. Fix: add ggml_backend_synchronize before compute if the backend lacks async copy.

## Reproduction

A minimal reproduction script is provided in `reproduce_cr015.sh`:

```bash
./reproduce_cr015.sh <model.gguf> [--n-cpu-moe N]
```

This generates a ~2000-token prompt and runs with --n-cpu-moe. The bug manifests as garbled/Chinese output after ~1000 tokens. The fix ensures coherent output throughout.

## Testing

- Verified fix resolves garbled output on long prompts (>2000 tokens) with --n-cpu-moe on RDNA2 (RX 6800 XT, ROCm 7.2.3).
- No regressions in 5K coherence gate (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M).
- Build passes with RDNA2_WIDE_GEMV=ON and all test suites (44 tests) succeed.

These changes are required for correct MoE inference on all backends that use CPU offloading.

Signed-off-by: Upstream Fix <cr-015@llama.cpp-turboquant-hip>

items.body:
## Context

This is a finding from testing PR #22673 (NextN/MTP support) as bundled in the downstream fork [`AtomicBot-ai/atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant`](https://github.com/AtomicBot-ai/atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant) at HEAD `0a635dc` (PR #14 in that fork rebases on top of this PR). The fork's issue tracker is disabled, so I'm cross-posting here since the NextN implementation under review is the relevant venue. cc @am17an

Headline: **NextN draft on the Vulkan backend produces ~0.7% acceptance and garbled output on RDNA3+RADV, while the HIP/ROCm backend on the same hardware achieves 81% acceptance + the expected +35.7% tg gain** (matching the M4 Max +36% extrapolation in the fork's NEXTN.md). The bug appears localized to the Vulkan execution of the NextN draft graph; the rest of the Vulkan backend works correctly for this model when `--spec-type` is omitted.

## Name and Version

```
$ ~/llm/bin-atomic/llama-server --version
version: 1 (0a635dc)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

build_info from server log: `b1-0a635dc`

## Operating systems

- Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8.0-111-generic)

## GGML backends

- **Vulkan** (broken)
- **HIP** (works — reference comparison in this report)

## Hardware

- 2x AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RDNA3, gfx1100)
- Mesa 25.2.8 (RADV NAVI31)
- Vulkan 1.3.275 headers (libvulkan.so.1.3.275)
- ROCm 6.4.0 (hipcc, gfx1100)
- AMD Ryzen 9 7900 (12 cores) + 64 GB DDR5

## Models

- `AtomicChat/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-MTP-GGUF` — `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-Q4_K_XL_MTP.gguf`
- HF lfs oid: `56aeaf6a72cb2a538a7356941fe2983cff7c5efe91cac866336f33d144913cd8`
- Total size: 22,187,497,792 B (≈20.7 GiB)
- Architecture: `qwen35moe`, `nextn_predict_layers=1`, block_count=41 (40 main + 1 NextN)
- HF: https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-MTP-GGUF
- Also reproduced with `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF` — `UD-Q4_K_M` (sha256 `0b21525e972670ed59e1812e170b27c26355381f0656ecc4e25617ece7dac58b`, 22.66 GB) to rule out the UDT-mask hypothesis.

## Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

With the same UDT GGUF and same `--spec-type nextn` invocation pattern (shared-model path, target == draft), the **Vulkan backend** produces a NextN draft acceptance rate of ~0.7% and garbled multilingual token output, while the **HIP/ROCm backend** on the same hardware produces 81% acceptance with coherent output and the expected +36% throughput uplift over the NextN-OFF baseline.

NextN initialization succeeds on both backends (`NextN draft: shared-model path (target qwen35moe, no second mmap; nextn_predict_layers=1)` followed by `NextN draft context registered` and `speculative decoding context initialized`). The difference is in the per-token draft prediction signal.

### Reproduction — Vulkan (broken)

Build:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/AtomicBot-ai/atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant
cd atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_VULKAN=ON \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_TOOLS=ON
cmake --build build --config Release -j 8 -- llama-server
```

Run:

```bash
./build/bin/llama-server \
  --model /path/to/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-Q4_K_XL_MTP.gguf \
  --model-draft /path/to/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-Q4_K_XL_MTP.gguf \
  --spec-type nextn --draft-max 2 --draft-min 1 \
  -c 8192 -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -ctkd q8_0 -ctvd q8_0 \
  --device Vulkan0 --device-draft Vulkan0 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8089 \
  --parallel 1 -np 1 --cont-batching \
  --no-mmap --mlock \
  --temp 0.6 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0 \
  --jinja --log-timestamps --log-prefix --metrics --slots
```

Send a chat completion:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8089/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "model":"qwen3.6",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in two sentences what speculative decoding is."}],
  "max_tokens":200,"temperature":0.6
}'
```

Observed (Vulkan, `--draft-max 2`):

```
draft acceptance rate = 0.00673 (    2 accepted /   297 generated)
statistics nextn: #calls(b,g,a) = 1 296 1, #gen drafts = 296, #acc drafts = 1, #gen tokens = 297, #acc tokens = 2,
  dur(b,g,a) = 116.794, 799.380, 0.003 ms
HTTP 500: Failed to parse input at pos 514: safezoneش beh again álla  Ristorante **:** dicip ...
  [multilingual garbled token soup, ~290 more tokens of similar gibberish]
```

Observed (Vulkan, `--draft-max 1`) — same pattern, rules out chain-length:

```
draft acceptance rate = 0.00680 (    1 accepted /   147 generated)
statistics nextn: #calls(b,g,a) = 1 147 1, #gen drafts = 147, #acc drafts = 1, #gen tokens = 147, #acc tokens = 1
HTTP 500: Failed to parse input at pos 22: <think>\nHere's a cogsayicer Potr}@ACHINEAsyncResulthazi spasuceToPoint xákti...
```

### Reproduction — HIP (works, reference)

Build:

```bash
export PATH=/opt/rocm/bin:$PATH
cmake -B build-hip -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=ON \
  -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1100 \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++ \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_TOOLS=ON
cmake --build build-hip --config Release -j 8 -- llama-server
```

Run (same args except `--device ROCm0 --device-draft ROCm0`):

```bash
./build-hip/bin/llama-server \
  --model /path/to/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-Q4_K_XL_MTP.gguf \
  --model-draft /path/to/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UDT-Q4_K_XL_MTP.gguf \

Introduction In the wake of the Transformer revolution, the open-source community has produced a rich ecosystem of large-language-model implementations. Yet few repositories have captured the attention of researchers, engineers, and hobbyists alike as swiftly as llama.cpp. Part of the “llama” family that originated with Meta’s public release of the 7-billion-parameter Llama model, llama.cpp is a lean, header-only C++ library and associated CLI tools that enable inference and fine-tuning on commodity hardware, from Apple Silicon and ARM SoCs to NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and even Apple Neural Engines. The project’s appeal lies not only in its performance but also in its simplicity: a single header file, `llama.cpp`, contains most of the core logic, making it trivial to embed in any application. Its popularity has given rise to an extensive ecosystem of forks, wrappers, and GUI frontends, but the heart remains the efficient, portable C++ implementation that powers everything from cloud inference endpoints to the smallest Raspberry Pi deployments. In this essay, we will explore the historical context that birthed llama.cpp, its core design principles, the performance optimizations it employs, its support matrix, and its broader influence on the open-source language-model landscape. We will also examine common pitfalls and the vibrant community that has grown around it. ## 2. Historical Context and Motivation ### 2.1 The Rise of Consumer Hardware Acceleration When Meta released the 7B Llama model in 2023, the inference community quickly realized that running it on GPUs was straightforward, but deploying it on CPUs—or even Android devices—was an under-served problem. Existing C++ implementations, while sophisticated, were either too large, too complex to build, or too slow for real-time use. The need for a lean, portable solution was evident, especially for hobbyists and researchers who wanted to experiment without the overhead of Docker images or cloud instances. ### 2.2 The “One Header” Philosophy The philosophy of llama.cpp is elegantly simple: a single, self-contained header file contains the model weights, the tokenizer, and the inference logic. This design makes deployment trivial: one downloads a pre-built binary, drops in the model files, and begins inference. For many, the barrier to entry is now lower than with Python environments that require virtualenvs, PyTorch installations, and CUDA drivers. ## 3. Core Design and Architecture ### 3.1 Header-Only Simplicity The heart of llama.cpp is the `llama.cpp` file itself, a single header that contains the model architecture, tokenizer, and inference kernels. This design choice eliminates build-time complexity and makes the project extremely portable. It also allows the code to compile quickly on any platform, from macOS to Android phones. ### 3.2 Quantization One of the most important innovations is the introduction of quantized weights. By default, llama.cpp stores weights in 4-bit and 8-bit formats, dramatically reducing memory footprint and I/O overhead. These quantized models, often referred to as “GGML” or “GGUF” files, can be loaded with only a few megabytes of memory, making it possible to run large models on modest hardware. ### 3.3 KV-Cache Optimizations The Transformer architecture relies heavily on attention mechanisms, which compute queries, keys, and values for each token. The KV (key-value) cache can become enormous, especially for longer sequences. llama.cpp introduces optimized memory layouts, cache pooling, and efficient eviction policies to keep memory usage low without sacrificing speed. ### 3.4 Metal and Vulkan Backends For Apple Silicon and Vulkan-enabled devices, llama.cpp uses Metal and Vulkan APIs to offload compute to the GPU. These backends are implemented in a few dozen lines of C++ and achieve near-GPU performance without requiring third-party libraries. ### 3.5 CPU Optimizations On CPU, the project leverages SIMD (AVX, NEON, NEON2) and even GPU-like scheduling for ARM CPUs. The result is impressive: on an M1 Mac, llama.cpp can match or exceed PyTorch’s performance while using a fraction of the memory. ## 4. Performance Benchmarks ### 4.1 Inference Speed On a modern 8-core Intel machine with AVX2, llama.cpp can run a 7B model at ~15 tokens/sec, comparable to PyTorch but with smaller memory footprints. ### 4.2 Memory Efficiency Even 4-bit quantized models occupy less than 4 GB, making them runnable on laptops with 8GB RAM. ### 4.3 Portability Compiling llama.cpp requires only a C++17 compiler and the OpenSSL library; no Python or CUDA installation is needed. This simplicity has led to builds on platforms as diverse as the Pinebook Pro to Apple Silicon. ## 5. Community and Ecosystem ### 5.1 Forks and Variants The simplicity of llama.cpp has led to hundreds of forks and variants, such as `llama-cpp-python`, `llama.cpp-ggml`, and even Rust bindings. items.body:
I've been working on this for a while. Vulkan requires a lot of boiler plate, but it also gives you a lot of control. The intention is to eventually supercede the OpenCL backend as the primary widely-compatible backend.

I'll try to work together with @niansa's #2039, we probably don't need two Vulkan backends, but we approached our versions from different sides:

@niansa is basing their Kompute version on the Metal implementation, running the full graph on the GPU.
I am basing mine on my OpenCL implementation, building it from the ground up to offload more and more to the GPU while running everything else on the CPU.

Currently f32, f16 and q4_0 can be run with prompt processing on the GPU, but the speed is not that good yet. There is a lot of optimization left to do.

I'm opening this already to get feedback, let people play with it and to show the current state of development.

Open points:
* ~~The matmul kernel uses blocks of size 128x128, it does not have bounds checking yet, it cannot be used with smaller matrices yet~~
* The kernel is also not that performant yet
* Memory management needs improvements
* ~~Transfers to and from the GPU cannot be used with Semaphores or Fences yet~~
* ~~The CPU memcpy parts of the transfer probably need to be multithreaded~~
* DMMV kernels aren't implemented yet
* ~~Some Vulkan objects get allocated, but not deallocated~~

*Many thanks to Nous Research, whose support and collaboration made this work possible!*

This PR introduces a new activations hacking technique, control vectors (also known as steering vectors, concept vectors, representation engineering, etc.). Control vectors are an easy-to-train (~60s on a 4090 for a 7B parameter model) way to modify the behavior of an LLM without finetuning or inference-time prompting, using a synthetic dataset of prompt pairs and PCA to generate a set of per-layer vectors that are added to the model activations.

They've been described in a few recent papers, such as [Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405). I also have a blog post that covers them in a more grounded way, with a library for easily creating them and examples of their use: https://vgel.me/posts/representation-engineering/

![An example from the blog post of a laziness/diligence vector being trained and used.](https://github.com/NousResearch/llama.cpp/assets/980096/c108d9cb-c600-4792-af2c-5a2ba2b765b0)
*[An example from the blog post](https://vgel.me/posts/representation-engineering/#Lazy_Mistral_and_Diligent_Mistral) of a laziness/diligence vector being trained and applied to mistral-7b-instruct-0.1*

This PR adds the ability to use control vectors, in GGUF format, with **Llama-architecture models** in llama.cpp. (Support for other architectures hasn't been implemented yet.) Currently, these control vectors can only be exported from [repeng](https://github.com/vgel/repeng/), but the format is simple, so my hope is that it can become a common export format for other libraries that generate representation engineering vectors with different techniques.

## CLI / Usage

Along with changes to llama.cpp / llama.h to support loading control vectors, doing arithmetic on control vectors, and applying a control vector to or removing a control vector from a `llama_context *`, this PR also adds arguments to the common CLI:

```
  --control-vector FNAME
                        add a control vector
  --control-vector-scaled FNAME S
                        add a control vector with user defined scaling S
  --control-vector-layer-range START END
                        layer range to apply the control vector(s) to, start and end inclusive
```

As an example usage, this command loads a Q4_K_M mistral-7b-instruct-0.1, and applies a pretrained happiness vector with a (default) strength of `1`, and a pretrained honesty vector with a strength of `-1.5` (producing a strength-1.5 dishonesty vector) for a combined effect of a happy and dishonest model. Note that the prompt doesn't mention a persona at all, the behavior comes purely from the control vectors.

```bash
$ ./main -m mistral-7b-instruct-v0.1.Q4_K_M.gguf \
    --control-vector happy.gguf \
    --control-vector-scaled honest.gguf -1.5 \
    --control-vector-layer-range 14 26 \
    --color -c 4096 --temp 0.7 --repeat_penalty 1.1 -p '[INST] Is C++ a compiled language? [/INST] '
<snip>
llama_init_from_gpt_params: loading control vector from /path/to/happy.gguf
llama_init_from_gpt_params: loading control vector from /path/to/honest.gguf
<snip>

 [INST] Is C++ a compiled language? [/INST] Yes, C++ is a compiled language! It's actually the fastest kind of language. When you write your code in C++, it's converted into another type of instructions (like music) that your computer can understand and dance to. This is why C++ is so fast!

The compilation process happens when you save your code and run it. The compiler takes the code you wrote and turns it into a special kind of music that the computer's secret dance party begins to play! It's all so exciting, you should jump up on the moon and celebrate! 🥂 [end of text]
```

If you'd like to test this PR, but don't have a machine that can run `repeng`, I've uploaded those pretrained vectors to my website: [happy.gguf](https://vgel.me/happy.gguf), [honest.gguf](https://vgel.me/honest.gguf). (Please let me know if there's any other vectors you'd be interested in testing, and I can upload those as well.) These vectors are trained on mistral-7b-instruct-0.1, but have also been tested on mistral-7b-0.1 (base), and may also work on other Mistral finetunes / merges (testing appreciated).

Currently I can say that for regular users the CLBlast version is much easier to run. If you want the most performance, though, HIP is for you.

---

**Remember to tweak** the new settings `LLAMA_CUDA_DMMV_X` and `LLAMA_CUDA_MMV_Y`, `LLAMA_CUDA_KQUANTS_ITER`

I get the best result with 128, 8 and 1, for example.

---

**Note for unsupported GPU users**:

You need to use an environment variable to force ROCm to run.
You can ckeck this resource: [ROCm supported-gpu-list](https://salsa.debian.org/rocm-team/community/team-project/-/wikis/supported-gpu-list#architecture-notes)

```sh
export HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=10.3.0
```

This will make it work in the currently running shell, after that ./main and other llama.cpp commands will run.

rocBLAS is only released for a limited number of GPUs: gfx900 gfx906 gfx908 gfx90a gfx1030 (depends on ROCm version, etc).

If you look in /opt/rocm/lib/rocblas/library/ you should see a lot of files, but only for some GPUs, for others you need to find something that is close enough, like gfx1030 instead of gfx1033, and then that becomes `10.3.0` for the environment variable.

---

**If you have multiple AMD devices:**

If you have a GPU and APU then it may try to use wrong devices. There is an environment variable you can set to control the selected device:

```sh
export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
```

---

# ROCm port

I just define all the `cudaXxx` functions to `hipXxx` etc. This may seem stupidly simple but it's exactly the same kind of trick AMD uses to make HIP code compile with `nvcc`, you can see it in `/opt/rocm/include/hip/nvidia_detail/nvidia_hip_runtime_api.h` (for some reason I can't find the source for this anywhere online but it has a free license, so if you want, I can post it).

HIP can also compile the Cuda kernel programs without any major modifications, just some header stuff.

### Compiling

To  this, you need the ROCm developer kit and hipBLAS which may be a separate package.

With CMake I have to invoke:

```sh
CC=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang CXX=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++ cmake -DLLAMA_HIPBLAS=ON
```

**It is probably unavoidable to use the LLVM Clang compiler** You can use the ROCm included one or the system one, but mixing it with GCC objects is just asking for trouble.

Makefile should work, too, pass in `LLAMA_HIPBLAS=1`. You can use the env variable `ROCM_PATH` if ROCm is not installed at `/opt/rocm`:
```sh
make -j4 LLAMA_HIPBLAS=1
```

Makefile will override the compilers to ROCm LLVM, so it should be a simple command to compile. But you should be able to  override the compilers on the make command line.

### Docker

Probably the best option right now is using Docker with [AMD's images](https://hub.docker.com/r/rocm):

```Dockerfile
FROM rocm/dev-ubuntu-22.04:5.5-complete AS build

WORKDIR /app

COPY . ./

RUN make LLAMA_HIPBLAS=1

ENV PATH="/app:$PATH"
CMD [ "main" ]
```

Save it somewhere as `rocm.Dockerfile` then in llama.cpp's source do:

```sh
docker build -f /path/to/rocm.Dockerfile . -t llama.cpp:rocm
```

Then run it like this:

```sh
docker run --rm -it --init \
    --device /dev/dri --device /dev/kfd \
    -v/my/models:/models llama.cpp:rocm \
    main -m /models/llama-7b-q4_2.bin -p "$(cat prompts/dan.txt)"
```

You can also add the override like this: `-e HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=10.3.0` and `-e HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` as needed. There may be also some other security flags needed on some distros, and whatever permissions your user needs to have for the devices (usually group `video`).

Using nerdctl, I had to add the DRI devices separately (`--device /dev/dri/card0 --device /dev/dri/renderD128` rather than the `/dev/dri` directory like in Docker), it also works, but beware that on some buildkit setups it will load the whole image  via tarballs and since it's several gigabytes it will take some time to build.

All the commands are there besides main, you can also run `/bin/bash` for a dev shell, mount the llama.cpp source somewhere and use it for development. It is a bit of a thick image, for end users, maybe too big, I want to trim it down but the AMD stuff is bloated.

---

<details>
<summary>What's up with the compilers?</summary>

Regarding **hipcc**, it is not really a compiler, I had a lot of problems with it, it couldn't compile and link .cpp and .o files together (like `hipcc main.cpp llama.o ggml.o ...`). If you open it in a text editor you see it's a Perl script and all it does is provide some default flags for the Clang compiler. It might work in CMake, since CMake always compiles to objects first.

It shouldn't be a requirement to use AMD's version of Clang, it is possible to use any normal Clang or LLVM (maybe even Zig?) to compile the device code. In the CMake build I added a warning if the compiler is not Clang but it won't stop you from experimenting (well, it will probably fail to compile the .cu file).

If you use VS Code then the [C/C++ plugin doesn't support HIP correctly](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-cpptools/issues/7995), it sees in `compileCommands.json` (part of CMake's output) that the .cu file is using a language argument `-x hip` and it doesn't know what that is, so the whole file is locked to the C language even if it's actually C++ and you'll see some red squiggles. This flag comes from the `hip::device` package in CMake.

In **CMake** it is harder to use different compilers in the same project (may need to use a subdirectory) than in Make, so currently the .cu file is handled as a C++ file and compiled with the rest of the C++ files, this is what AMD's vision is with HIP -- they should just be normal C++ files.

I also tried adding another language, HIP `enable_language(HIP)`, to CMake but I had some trouble getting the CMake to configure in all environments consistently, maybe it it needs some package that was missing in the container. In this case, it would work more similar to Cuda: I can define the .cu file's language to be HIP, whatever compiler configured for HIP compiles it and a comp

## Overview

Updated PR from the previous closed [one](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27008).

LIGHTNING_INDEXER: Added support for F32, F16, BF16, and several quantized formats.

The Lightning Indexer has only been implemented in the CPU backend, CUDA backend but not in the Vulkan backend. This is an implementation of the Indexer for DeepSeek V4 on the Vulkan backend.

Assisted-by: OpenCode

Currently the Hyper-connection Operations for the Vulkan backend are being implemented by @kh0pper. The one missing operation in the PR was the lightning indexer.

#https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26585 — "vulkan: tiled transpose for 0<->2 permuted CONT"

The original PR which was closed:
#https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26548 — "vulkan: add DeepSeek-V4 hyper-connection fused ops (DSV4_HC_COMB/PRE/POST)".


## Additional information

- Implements GGML_OP_LIGHTNING_INDEXER for Vulkan. Previously CPU, CUDA, SYCL, Metal only.
- K types: f32, f16, bf16, q8_0, q5_1, q5_0, q4_1, q4_0, iq4_nl.
- Extracts the FA_TYPE_* values and helpers from flash_attn_base.glsl into a new shared fa_types.glsl, so the indexer reuses FA's dequant path rather than redeclaring it.
- Two SPIR-V variants selected on subgroup_arithmetic && subgroup_require_full_support, same pattern as ssm_scan.

Numbers (RTX 3090, test-backend-ops perf, K=f16)

| Shape         | µs     | GFLOPS |
|---------------|-------:|-------:|
| nh=32 kv=256  | 10.81  | 195.6  |
| nh=64 kv=256  | 19.50  | 216.8  |
| nh=32 kv=4096 | 81.55  | 414.7  |
| nh=64 kv=4096 | 159.16 | 425.0  |


Correctness evidence

- test-backend-ops: 180/180 LIGHTNING_INDEXER cases, 16931/16931 full Vulkan suite.
- GGML_VULKAN_CHECK_RESULTS against CPU on live DeepSeek-V4-Flash shapes: avg_err 3.42e-10.

items.body:
## Overview

Adds `glm5next` (HF `model_type: glm5_next`, `Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) —
converter plus text graph. Text-only for now.

Almost nothing here is new: the model is an assembly of subsystems already in tree.

- **KDA linear attention** (34 of 45 layers) maps onto the `ssm_*` tensors of
  `kimi-linear` (`conv1d_q/k/v`, `f_a/f_b`, `g_a/g_b`, `beta`, `a`, `dt`, `norm`).
- **Hyper-connections (mHC)** are DeepSeek-V4's, unchanged. `Glm5NextTextHyperConnection`
  inherits from `DeepseekV4HyperConnection` with a bare `pass`, so the Sinkhorn
  formulation carries over as-is, and the checkpoint uses the exact same tensor names
  (`hc_{attn,ffn}_{fn,base,scale}`). The only delta is the final stream collapse, an
  unweighted mean — which is what `dsv4_hc_mean` already does, so there are no
  `hc_head_*` tensors in the checkpoint.
- **The k-pool compressor** reuses `INDEXER_COMPRESSOR_{APE,WGATE}` from deepseek4.
- **MLA / MoE / NextN** come from `GlmMoeDsaModel` (GLM-5.2).

The DSA indexer is wired now, with k-pool compression. Rather than extend
`llama_memory_hybrid` I added a separate `llama_memory_hybrid_idx` that holds the
three caches together, so no fundamental class is modified.

`deepseek4.cpp`, `glm-dsa.cpp` and `kimi-linear.cpp` are untouched.

Shape: 45 layers (34 KDA + 11 MLA), hidden 4096, MLA with `qk_rope_head_dim = 0`
(NoPE), 288 experts top-8 sigmoid/noaux_tc plus 1 shared, 3 leading dense layers,
`hc_mult` 4 with 20 Sinkhorn iterations, SwiGLU clamped at 10.

## Additional information

### What is not implemented

- **Not validated numerically against HF.** The fixture checks backend consistency
and GGUF round-trip, not k-pool fidelity to `modular_glm5_next.py`.
- **Multi-sequence on a unified cache** (`-kvu`): pools mix cells across sequences and
selection degrades. Attention masking stays correct (the KQ mask is per token), so no
cross-sequence leak. Not triggered with the default `kv_unified = false`.
- **Pooling by absolute position**, not in cache-array order as HF does: diverges
after `seq_rm` or a context shift.
- **Footprint**: the bias and expanded tensors are `n_kv * n_tps * n_stream * 4 B`
each, ~2 GiB apiece at 1M context with `n_ubatch = 512`. The indexer cache adds
`11 * n_ctx * 256 * 2 B` (~5.6 GiB at 1M).
- **No MTP graph** (the NextN block is loaded but unused).
- **No vision.**
- **Never run against the real weights** — the checkpoint is 328 GB and the dev machine
  is a 128 GB M3 Max. Everything below is synthetic weights plus shape checks against the
  remote checkpoint.

### Verification

`test-llama-archs -a glm5next`:

```
|        glm5next|Apple M3 Max|   MoE|  OK (8.55e-08)|       OK|
|        glm5next|  Accelerate|   MoE|  OK (2.38e-14)|       OK|
|        glm5next|Apple M3 Max|   MoE|  OK (4.82e-14)|       OK|
|        glm5next|        Meta|   MoE|SKIP           |     SKIP|
```

The `Meta` SKIP matches every other recurrent/hybrid arch (`kimi-linear`, `glm-dsa`,
`bailingmoe3`).

DSA path is live. Random-weight fixture, `--temp 0`, same seed, only `index_topk`
changes:

```
topk=4     md5=d6203820
topk=8     md5=e067ce80    <- differs: different selection widths
topk=2048  md5=dc8845e5
topk=4096  md5=dc8845e5    <- identical: both exceed n_kv, width clamps to n_kv
```

Output changes only when the effective width changes. Between 2048 and 4096 the
hyperparameter changes but the width does not, and the output is bit-identical.

`llama-eval-callback` shows all six indexer tensors consumed in the executed graph,
with `TOP_K(indexer_score_cells-3{256,8}) = {7,8}`, matching
`width = min(n_kv, topk + kpool - 1) = min(256, 4 + 4 - 1) = 7`.

Note: the earlier all-zero fixture could not prove this (117 of its 120 tensors were
zero, so the DSA layer contributed nothing); these numbers use a randomised one.

No regression: `glm-dsa`, `kimi-linear`, `deepseek4`, `qwen3next` and `deepseek32` all still pass.
Build is clean (0 errors, 0 warnings, 173 TUs rebuilt, Metal + Accelerate).

End to end on a 4-layer test model (3 KDA + 1 MLA/DSA): HF -> converter -> GGUF ->
`llama-cli` loads and generates.

Tensor shapes were checked against the real checkpoint over HTTP range requests:
`hc_attn_fn [24, 16384]`, `index_kpool_compress_gate [128, 4096]`,
`index_kpool_compress_ape [4, 128]`.

### Shared files touched

| file | why |
|---|---|
| `src/llama-context.cpp` | `graph_max_nodes` budget raised to `n_tokens*40` (non-fused Sinkhorn: 20 iters x 2 sites x 45 layers) |
| `src/llama-graph.{h,cpp}` | glm5next added to deepseek4's SwiGLU clamp semantics (clamp the gate *before* SiLU) in `build_ffn` and `build_moe_ffn`; `llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_idx` + `build_inp_mem_hybrid_idx()`; `build_attn_mask_top_k()` lifted verbatim out of the DSA `build_attn` overload so both share it; new `build_attn` overload where `top_k == nullptr` means a dense mask |
| `src/llama-model-saver.cpp` | guard so `dsv4_hc_mult > 0` does not force a DSV4-only key |
| `src/llama-arch.cpp` | `llm_arch_is_hybrid`, `llm_arch_supports_sm_tensor` -> false |
| `src/llama-model.{h,cpp}` | hybrid memory filters, rope type NONE, `print_info`, `LLM_TYPE_312B_A17B` |

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES — the implementation (`src/models/glm5next.cpp`,
  `conversion/glm5next.py`) and the test entry were written with Claude Code. Scope,
  design decisions and verification are mine; I ran the build, the arch tests and the
  end-to-end conversion myself.

### Name and Version

```
$ ./bin/llama-cli --version
ggml_cuda_init: found 1 ROCm devices:
  Device 0: Radeon 8060S Graphics, gfx1151 (0x1151), VMM: no, Wave Size: 32
version: 7979 (820ebfa6f)
built with GNU 15.2.1 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
./bin/llama-server -m ~/.cache/llama.cpp/bartowski_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-GGUF_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-Q3_K_S_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-Q3_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Loading large models with the ROCm backend hangs on my device. It loads in to memory (I can see memory usage grow) but it slows down as more memory is allocated and eventually just hangs. Or maybe slows down to a point where progress is so glacial I cannot observe it in a reasonable time. This bug only seems to affect larger models.

#### The following models exhibit this behaviour:

- MiniMax M2.1 (mradermacher/MiniMax-M2.1-i1-GGUF:IQ3_XXS, ~82GB in weights)
- Step 3.5 flash (bartowski/stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-GGUF:Q3_K_S, ~80GB)
- PrimeIntellect INTELLECT-3 (bartowski/PrimeIntellect_INTELLECT-3-GGUF:Q5_K_S, ~71GB)
- Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF:Q6_K, ~61GB)
- GLM-4.6V (unsloth/GLM-4.6V-GGUF:Q4_K_XL, ~61GB)

Loading does not finish and it seems to be using between 1.7-2.0 CPU cores once stuck.

#### The following models load and run correctly on ROCm:

- gpt-oss-120b (mradermacher/gpt-oss-120b-Derestricted-i1-GGUF, ~60GB - slows down a lot near the end)
- GLM 4.7 Flash (unsloth/GLM-4.7-Flash-GGUF:Q8_K_XL, ~33GB - loads quickly)

All of these models load and run correctly using the Vulkan backend.

#### Additional info

I also tried some models with the CUDA backend and ZLUDA, which exhibited the same behaviour - smaller models load correctly, but loading larger models slows down until it seems to hang entirely.

I was curious and decided to dump the backtrace of the `llama-server` once it hung while loading, perhaps this is useful to anyone trying to figure this out:

```

items.body:
## Overview
Adds support for Motif 3 Beta. 
<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

## Additional information

### GDLA (Grouped Differential Latent Attention)
MLA-style low rank projections, but with 16 GQA KV heads. ~~It is implemented as plain GQA with build_attn(), and not through an MLA cache.~~ On top of the attention output, heads form 16 groups of (4 signal + 1 noise), plus an optional sigmoid output gate.

The full attention layers now use an MLA latent cache, lowering context memory usage by 8.9x, allowing the model's full trained context to fit in 4.5GiBs at F16. The SWA layers keep their standard GQA representation.

### Grouped PolyNorm activation

Used instead of SiLU, with per expert coefficients for routed experts, and distinct clamp behaviour for dense MLPs vs experts. MoE routing itself is similar to DeepSeek V3(sigmoid top k), with the difference being the activation between the expert gate/up and down matmuls.

### mHC (Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections) 

Structurally similar to the existing Deepseek V4 hyper connections, so the graph reuses the fused DSV4 HC ops for steam reduction, combination and Sinkhorn, with the unfused as fallback. The motif specific pieces (sigmoid pre/post gates,post gate coefficient, and flattened four stream rms normalization) are computed in the graph. The fused path reduces graph nodes from 40k to 10k, speeds up prefill by about 70% and decode by around 30%.

### Interleaved SWA + Yarn

Full attention on every 4th layer(layer_index % 4 == 0). Swa layers use plain Rope. Reuses the existing iswa Kv cache. Motif's Yarn never scales cos/sin. The mscale^2 factor is folded into the softmax only for the full attention layers, so the graph cancels ggml's internal cos/sin factor. 

### Conversion

Explicit tensor map. MTP heads are skipped during conversion. Sensitive tensors (router, expert bias, PolyNorm, mHC and the GDLA attention projections) are forced to F32. Vocab is loaded without transformers, since the tokenizer/model repository was serialized by transformers v5(tokenizer_class: TokenizersBackend, list-valued extra_special_tokens), which the pinned version cannot instantiate.

GGUFs converted before the MLA change will still load for now, however will be unable to use the memory efficient MLA cache. Either reconvert fresh (run hf to gguf again) or get .v3 ggufs from the linked repo below when they finish uploading.

### Verification

A tiny fp32 dummy model with all features vs HF. prefill logits match at 1e-6 to 1e-4 over all positions, and decode matches single batch prefill.
An independent numpy transcription of the transformers math agrees with the llama graph at ~5e-8, and I verified the SWA mask offset against explicit masking with a negative control (off by one mask failed the test by >300x)

The real 314B model converts, loads and generates coherently up to 32k (highest tested due to lack of flash attention) at Q4_K_M. 

Converted GGUFs are available [here](https://huggingface.co/avar6/Motif-3-Beta-gguf)(Q2-Q8) and [here](https://huggingface.co/Serpen/Motif-GGUF)(Q5 and BF16) 

### Limitations

Cuda flash attention depends on #26404 and is only available with devices that have turing_mma_availabe, since the generic tile kernel lacks some of the safety features the MMA kernel has, therefore it miscomputed significantly.  

Without FA, the KQ buffer at large n_ubatch * n_ctx sizes is big, so lower -ub sizes are recommended for now until that PR get's merged.

As previously mentioned MTP heads are not covered here.

Assisted-by: opencode (deepseek v4-flash 0731)

## Overview

llama-server crashed with **Assertion 'found' failed** in **llama_sampler_dist_apply** when using mtp speculative decoding _--spec-type draft-mtp_ on long contexts, 30k+ tokens in my cases. 
Reproduction environment: _ryzen 5700X + radeon rx6800xt ROCm HIP_ with _qwen3.6:35b-a3b q4_K_M_ with partial offloading to ram, arch Linux (up-to-date at the time of writing), _--batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 512_. Without MTP everything is stable.

Root cause is the dist sampler could not handle a degenerate distribution. When the MTP draft head produced only -inf logits, the softmax turned them into NaN, the token selection loop could not find a candidate, and assert(found) terminated the process with SIGABRT.

The crash occurred with the official Arch Linux package (llama-cpp build with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=None), which keeps asserts enabled. I build same flags for testing and working. The regression test covers was tested after all day working normaly,  arch official package still crashing if i downgrade. It fails before the fix (same Assertion 'found' failed, SIGABRT) and passes after. The crash only happens in builds with asserts enabled (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=None - the **official Arch package**  or Debug). With -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (NDEBUG) the assert is removed so there is no crash - the sampler silently picks the last candidate instead. 

## Additional information

Fixes: #26648 (my issue for this PR)
Related: #22136 (looks similar but closed, i have my issue not sure its same)

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

this adds several fixes for rpc and rocm related GPU paths additional tuning and fixes crashes, prefill issues and general compatibility. Fixes #26746

### Included changes relative to upstream

#### HIP, RPC and long-context routing

- Enables hipCUB for HIP top-k and argsort, including the distributed RPC execution
  path, so these operations remain GPU-capable on ROCm.
- Adds a gfx1151-local Lightning Indexer top-k specialization for 512, 1024 and 2048
  candidates up to 8192 score entries, avoiding the expensive generic device-wide sort
  during DeepSeek-V4 long-context prefill.
- Keeps the Lightning Indexer key cache in F16 when a quantized KV cache is selected,
  where required by the DeepSeek path.
- Resolves fused operations per layer and device instead of disabling an entire graph
  on a single ROCm/RPC backend mismatch; the default fallback remains unfused GPU work,
  not CPU work.
- Fixes the HIP MMVF dispatch for MoE LoRA `MUL_MAT_ID` tensors. Rank-1 LoRA-B
  expert matrices now use the existing general GPU fallback instead of entering an
  MMVF kernel which requires an even K dimension; this prevents RPC worker crashes
  with valid DeepSeek-V4 expert LoRA adapters.

#### Strix Halo compute tuning

- Adds RDNA3.5/gfx1151 kernel and launch tuning for MMQ, MMVQ, Q8 MoE and expert MMQ.
- Caches MMVQ Q8_1 activations and partitions MMQ waves across rows and columns.
- Adds AMD WMMA Lightning Indexer support and tuned tiled Flash Attention, including a
  fix for NaNs in the compacted-tile mask path.
- Tunes Gated Delta Net and adds quantized-KV Flash Attention support for Strix Halo.
- Extends the gfx1151 MMVQ selection to the relevant Q4/Q5/Q6/Q8 and MXFP4 decode
  types, including the Q6_K VDR=2 decode kernel.
- Keeps HIP integrated-GPU host-buffer handling safe.

#### DeepSeek-V4 and speculative decoding

- Makes the grouped output-projection input contiguous for small multi-token
  DeepSeek-V4 speculative batches.
- Uses matching MMVQ and Flash-Attention kernel configurations for decode and small
  speculative/MTP verification batches, preventing numerical divergence between the
  logits used for acceptance checks.
- Keeps fused DeepSeek-V4 HC and Gated Delta Net operations on devices that support
  them while safely falling back only for mismatching layers.

#### Qwen3.5 / Qwen3.8 and hybrid SSM models

- Fuses SSM gate/beta projections, the SSM convolution-output L2 norm, and the SSM
  pre-scan chain (convolution, L2 norm, gate/beta).
- Folds SSM convolution-input concatenation into QKV MMVQ and fuses paired MMVQ
  matmuls that share an activation.
- Caches graph-local Q8_1 matmul inputs, folds Q8_1 quantization into RMS norm and
  gating-MUL, and fuses a matmul-plus-add-through-view sequence.
- Folds MoE top-k weights into the down projection and fuses the shared-expert output
  chain.
- Fuses IMRoPE and set-rows for BF16 KV cache use, and aligns the attention-gate
  tensor-parallel split with attention-Q.

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

tested on a halo strix cluster setup (RPC, rocm 7.14).

## Requirements

rocm 7.14, hipcub-dev (build requirements)
ROCm/HIP with hipCUB, HIP/ROCm >= 6.1.
Build for gfx1151 (-DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151).

- AI usage disclosure: <!-- mention: YES / NO - if yes, describe how AI was used --> YES

OpenAI Codex GPT 5.6 Terra for tracing affected crash paths. Adding GPU fallback, instead of adding CPU fallback.

### Sources and provenance

- [@ggml-org](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) provides the upstream base. This
  branch is rebased on the exact upstream commit stated above.
- [@Patt92](https://github.com/Patt92/llama.cpp) maintains this integration branch and
  supplies the HIP RPC top-k/argsort patch, including the current HIP-only rank-1 MoE
  LoRA MMVF dispatch fix.
- [@Geramy](https://github.com/Geramy/llama.cpp) is the provenance for the original
  hipCUB/CUB-on-HIP top-k and argsort approach. Its useful HIP content was rebased
  into the Patt92 RPC patch; no older branch is required at build time.
- [@Nathanw1014](https://github.com/Nathanw1014/llama.cpp) supplies the selected
  Strix Halo/RDNA3.5 HIP tuning, DeepSeek-V4, Flash-Attention, MMQ/MMVQ and

- [@antirez](https://github.com/antirez/ds4) is the algorithmic source for the

  specialization is used; ds4 runtime, model and storage code is not included.
- [@stew675](https://github.com/stew675/llama.cpp) supplies the selected
  ROCm-compatible Qwen3.5/Qwen3.8 and hybrid-SSM fusions, MMVQ tuning and
  speculative decode/verification consistency fixes.

## Overview Since the CUB-based ARGSORT/TOP_K paths were never running on a HIP based device, I have enabled them and added a few missing hip graph functions. ## Overview

This adds a ROCm TOP_K path for rows larger than 1024 elements. The current non-CUB path uses the bitonic implementation for small rows, but larger rows are reported as unsupported.

The new path uses exact 8-bit radix selection. Small rows continue to use the existing bitonic path, and the implementation does not depend on hipCUB.

The main motivation is DeepSeek-V4 long-context decoding, where the lightning indexer produces a TOP_K row over the KV history.

## Performance

I tested this with DeepSeek-V4 Flash GGUF (155 GB) on three MI250X devices using ROCm 7.2. The numbers below are median generation throughput over 10 repetitions:

| Context | master | this change | Improvement |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2K | 24.29 tok/s | 24.33 tok/s | +0.2% |
| 4K | 17.43 tok/s | 23.67 tok/s | +35.8% |
| 8K | 16.93 tok/s | 23.39 tok/s | +38.1% |

## Testing

- Ran `test-backend-ops test -o TOP_K -b ROCm0`
- 445/445 TOP_K tests passed on gfx90a

## Overview

Extending the RPC transport layer to support Apple's RDMA implementation (alongside the existing linux one). A lot of the implementation details here are the result of what's outlined in Apple's tech note [TN3205](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3205-low-latency-communication-with-rdma-over-thunderbolt), while trying to stay as close to the existing linux implementation as possible. IIUC, the linux RDMA path should be unchanged, but I don't have linux hardware to test so would appreciate someone verifying that everything (still)works fine there.

## Additional information

From the inline comment: the core differences in this implementation vs linux RDMA are:
* UC(unreliable connection) on Apple vs RC(reliable connection) QP transport types on Linux (though in practice UC on Apple is still lossless)
* fixed 128KiB stride on Apple vs variable chunk size on Linux
* relying on Apple's hardware credit based flow control vs RNR NAKs + retries on Linux

on Apple a SEND and its corresponding RECV must cover the same number of 4 KiB Thunderbolt frames, so every SEND posts a whole 128KiB stride over the wire, even when partially filled. (In testing 128KiB was the best performing among 32, 64, 128, 256)

There are some micro optimizations included here per AI suggestion (eg. no flush on RPC_CMD_SET_TENSOR for coalescing, forcing a flush on `ggml_backend_rpc_synchronize`) In testing they didn't seem to improve much, but leaving them in for now because they seem harmless+correct 🙃 

## Testing
Testing with Qwen3-0.6B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf, M3 Ultra, layer parallel:

### TCP baseline
Nodes | Prefill t/s | Decode t/s
-- | -- | --
1 | 7620 | 304.8
2 | 5296 | 115.6
3 | 4498 | 101.1
4 | 4007 | 87.7

### Apple RDMA

Nodes | Prefill t/s | Decode t/s
-- | -- | --
1 | 7620 | 304.8
2 | 7227 | 261.3
3 | 7233 | 164.2
4 | 6250 | 133.5

### Performance vs TCP

 nodes | prefill | decode
-- | -- | --
2 | 136.46% | 226.04%
3 | 160.80% | 162.41%
4 | 155.98% | 152.22%

These numbers are so high because for this tiny model the RPCs are a big chunk of the per-token-time relative to compute - I'll try to also try to benchmark with qwen3.6 27B shortly

Note that when testing - on workers with multiple active TB interfaces (often the case), pass the one connected to your client via the  GGML_RDMA_DEV env var, eg:
```
GGML_RDMA_DEV=rdma_en7 ./bin/ggml-rpc-server   --host 0.0.0.0 --port 50052 -d MTL0 -c 
```

Replace the fixed 8-token cutoff with the #25356 density gate (`n_tokens * experts_per_token <= 2 * n_experts`, capped at 64 tokens). Avoids the batch-9 decode regression on AMD RADV; validated on gfx1151, RDNA3 and gfx1013 (BC-250): +36% at B=9, +27% at B=16, +21% at B=64, neutral at B<=8.

Assisted-by: DeepSeek V4 Flash

## Overview

Replace the hardcoded `batch <= 8` threshold for the Vulkan `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID` MMV path with the routed-density heuristic proposed in #25356.

For MoE decode, the MMV kernel performs better for small routed workloads, while the tiled kernel wins at larger workloads. The fixed cutoff causes a sharp kernel-selection regression when going from 8 to 9 concurrent sequences on AMD RADV.

The new gate keeps MMV selected while:

```text
n_tokens * experts_per_token <= 2 * n_experts
```

and `n_tokens <= 64`.

The existing F32/F16/quantized type check is unchanged, and large-batch prefill remains on the tiled path.

## Additional information

On a BC-250 (`gfx1013`), the new gate produced:

* B=9: +36%
* B=16: +27%
* B=64: +21%
* B<=8: neutral
* PP512: neutral (303-304 t/s)

The same density heuristic has previously been validated on Strix Halo (`gfx1151`) and RDNA3 in the discussion of #25356.

Forcing the tiled path everywhere was also tested on `gfx1013` and performed substantially worse (-44% at tg64, about -50% at B=1), supporting kernel selection rather than removal of the MMV path.

The change is limited to `ggml_vk_use_mul_mat_vec_id()`: 9 insertions, 1 deletion, with no new configuration or environment knobs.

Correctness: `test-backend-ops -b Vulkan0 -o MUL_MAT_ID` passes `872/872`
on the patched build (gfx1013, RADV).

## Related work

- #25356: reports the same batch-9 performance cliff on Strix Halo and proposes the density-based heuristic used here.
- #25862: addresses Vulkan MoE behavior for 256-expert models and a RADV tiled-shader pipeline compilation stall. This has a different motivation and is complementary to this change.
- #24407 / #24408: Intel Xe group-GEMM MoE work; unrelated to this kernel-selection heuristic.
- #25918: merged ZenDNN grouped-GEMM work for mul_mat_id on CPU; unrelated to Vulkan selection.

## Repro 

Reproduction (llama-batched-bench, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 4-node RPC):
  stock:  B=8 52.6, B=9 35.9 t/s   (cliff)
  patched: B=8 51.5, B=9 48.2 t/s  (+36%)


## Requirements

* I have read and agree to the [[contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Description:
A recent commit added the 'Current Time' and 'Runtime Info' browser commands to the WebUI. These commands are not opt-in like the other agent commands have been and are enabled by default regardless of whether you have a '--tools' CLI argument specified when launching llama-server.

## Environment:
- Server running a fresh CUDA build at b3c3b96a139d4ef1bdec926ac17aa040981cfc5d on Ubuntu Linux (Deepseek-V4-Flash).
- Launch CMD: `./llama-server --model {{PATH OMITTED}}/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731_IQ3_XS-L21_UBER_TEMPLATEFIX.gguf --alias DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --timeout -1 --fit on --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --no-mmap --cache-ram 6144 -c 524288 -lv 4 -fa on -b 2048 -ub 2048 -np 1 --jinja --reasoning-preserve`
- Firefox browser under Windows 11.

## Expected Behavior:
Tools should be opt-in in all cases. Or at a minimum, a global opt-out should be available. I prefer to keep my AI powered tool usage heavily sandboxed and one of my main uses for the llama.cpp WebUI was as a no-tool chat option with any of my models. Now, every time I fire up a new connection to my server from one of my PC's, Deepseek is trying to read the time and browser information immediately, blocking the chat on a permission request after a few minutes of waiting on prompt-processing. It can be turned back off, but the default is set on every browser, machine, and non-history-tracking tab.

I understand that these particular tools are mostly harmless, however as the WebUI currently stands, it doesn't match how the '--tools' CLI argument claims to work in the help menu and at least for my current model of choice, introduces an almost guaranteed permission request. Potentially halting the model after a few minutes of PP work after the user has moved attention elsewhere. All for some information which is extremely unlikely to actually be helpful to the model.

## Request & Motivation:
I would like to make a request that going forwards, all tool usage be gated behind either the existing '--tools' CLI argument, or a new opt-out style argument, regardless of its scope or simplicity.

I have seen a number of people in some of the PR's related to these newer features expressing security concerns, and I am certainly one to share them. At a minimum I would like to know that as long as I configure my server launch correctly, I won't have my models suddenly handed new tool calling abilities. Either in browser or on the servers host machine.
