items.body:
### Summary

With `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` (GGUF) served by `llama-server` with `--jinja` and tools armed, generation **terminated mid-tag with `finish_reason: "stop"`** on three consecutive agent turns — each time exactly at the point where the reasoning stream contained literal DSML closing fragments (`</｜DSML｜parameter>`, `</｜DSML｜invoke>`). The final streamed token was `tool_c` — an *incomplete* `</｜DSML｜tool_calls>` closing tag. The client-visible result is an agent that appears to stop mid-tool-call, and (because the truncated message is persisted into history) a self-perpetuating loop: each follow-up turn imitates the truncated pattern and gets cut at the same place.

### Environment

- `llama-server` build 10573, commit `d775b8967` (master, 2026-08-22), AppleClang 21, Darwin arm64
- Backends: Metal (M5 Max) + one RPC worker (DGX Spark GB10), `--split-mode layer`
- Model: `unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF` UD-Q8_K_XL (5 shards) + `dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf` draft
- Flags: `--spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 3 -c 393216 --flash-attn on --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 --jinja --temp 0.6 --top-p 0.95`
- Effective slot state observed: `chat_format: "peg-native"`, `reasoning_format: "deepseek"`, `generation_prompt: "<｜Assistant｜><think>"`

### Observed (3 consecutive turns, harness session transcript)

| Turn | input tokens | output tokens | finish | stream ends at |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~165,000 | ~120 (est.) | stop | reasoning text `...a1b2c3d` + `</｜DSML｜parameter>` |
| 2 | 168,991 | 126 | stop | `...a1b2c3` + `</｜DSML｜parameter>\n</｜DSML｜invoke>\n</｜DSML｜tool_c` |
| 3 | 169,132 | 119 | stop | same fragment, same cut point |

Final reasoning deltas for turn 3 (verbatim, from the client event log):

```
... 'c', '3', '</｜DSML｜', 'parameter', '>', '\n', '</｜DSML｜', 'inv', 'oke', '>', '\n', '</｜DSML｜', 'tool', '_c'
```

The model was composing a file-edit tool call whose parameter value contained backtick-quoted hex strings (`` `a1b2c3d4e5f6` ``). The reasoning text shows the model interleaving protocol markup into the thinking channel; the stream then terminates *mid-tag*. No EOS content token is visible in the client stream — the stop appears to come from the serving side's handling of the DSML structure, not from a deliberate EOS the model wrote.

### Expected

Reasoning/thinking content should be treated as opaque text: a stray or partial DSML closing tag inside reasoning must not end generation. If the model truly opens a tool call, the parser should wait for a well-formed close; a malformed close should yield a parse error or plain text — never a silent mid-tag `stop`.

### Minimal repro attempt (negative result at short context)

A direct request asking the model to quote `</｜DSML｜parameter>` inside its reasoning, with a dummy tool armed, completed normally at short context (`finish: stop`, 271 completion tokens, tag quoted intact). So the failure is **not** triggered by the tag alone — the incidents happened at **~165–169K context depth** in an agentic multi-tool flow (the harness session had ~100 prior tool calls). Possibly depth-dependent (parser state / attention degradation at depth making the model emit protocol markup mid-reasoning more likely, and/or the parser's early-stop engaging once it does).

### Why it matters

The truncated message is persisted by clients as a normal completed turn (`finish: stop`), and the model then imitates its own truncated pattern on the next turn — the failure is self-reinforcing within a session. Three identical stops in a row required abandoning the session.

### Related

- vllm-project/vllm#48931 — DSML parser fragility when the model omits the `<｜DSML｜tool_calls>` START wrapper (V4, long context)
- ggml-org/llama.cpp#25618 — draft-dspark/draft-mtp greedy divergence on quantized targets
- ggml-org/llama.cpp#26554 — DSpark + V4-Flash long-generation abort

Happy to provide the full client event log (JSONL), server logs, or test patches.

This is a draft that we will keep iterating on: the description and commit messages will be revised before marking ready for review.

Adds two Metal matmul kernels for small batches (8 < `ne11` <= 32) — the speculative-decoding verify/draft regime:

- `kernel_mul_mm_s`: `mul_mm` with 32x16 tiles instead of 64x32. The stock tile pads N to 32 and launches `ne01/64` threadgroups, which under-fills the GPU at these sizes (on M3/M4, `pp16 == pp32` in wall time).
- split-K variant (4 slices) for shapes with few row tiles. Partials are written to scratch at the tail of the dst allocation (same pattern as `mul_mat_id`) and summed by a fixed-order reduce, so results are deterministic.

Kernel selection is unchanged by default: mv-ext keeps `ne11` 2..8, the mm branch keeps its stock break-even and uses the new tiles for 8 < `ne11` <= 32. `ne11` > 32 and tensor-API devices (M5+) use the stock path. `GGML_METAL_MM_SKINNY_MAX=0` restores stock behavior; `GGML_METAL_MM_SPLITK`, `GGML_METAL_MM_MIN`, `GGML_METAL_MV_EXT_MAX/_R1` are available for tuning.

Companion to #27383 — DSpark verify/draft batches run at `ne11` ~ 8..16. The kernels themselves are model-independent.

Numbers so far (M4 Max, 36 GB): `llama-bench -p 10` on LFM2.5-2.6B F16 goes 334 -> 460 t/s; end-to-end speculative decoding on a 150-prompt suite at temp 0 goes 1.84x -> 2.27x mean speedup, accept length unchanged. tg and large-batch pp are unaffected. Split-K changes f16 summation order, so occasional greedy ties differ from the stock kernel; outputs are bit-reproducible run to run.

End-to-end speculative decoding, this branch + #27383 merged (LFM2.5-2.6B F16 target + block-9 DSpark drafter, M4 Max, temp 0, speedup vs the same server without spec flags; accept length identical between configs):

| dataset | accept | stock | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| math500 (n=20) | 4.45 | 1.79x | 2.26x |
| humaneval (n=20) | 5.24 | 2.04x | 2.62x |
| mtbench (n=10) | 3.33 | 1.28x | 1.62x |

With the block-7 drafters linked from #27383 the verify batch is 8 tokens (`ne11` = 8, outside the changed range) and speedups are unchanged (1.85x vs 1.87x mean) — block-9 LFM2.5 drafter GGUFs are being published.

`test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT -b Metal` passes with the new paths enabled and disabled.

llama-bench on this branch, M4 Max 36GB (`-p 8,10,16,32 -n 16 -b 32 -ub 32 -fa 1 -r 3`), t/s stock (`GGML_METAL_MM_SKINNY_MAX=0`) → this PR:

| model | pp8 | pp10 | pp16 | pp32 | tg16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| LFM2.5-2.6B-F16 | 291 → 292 | 353 → 478 | 563 → 804 | 1138 → 1316 | 64 → 64 |
| LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-F16 | 662 → 658 | 794 → 1107 | 1258 → 1768 | 2563 → 2946 | 142 → 142 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-F16 | 201 → 201 | 247 → 307 | 386 → 507 | 790 → 858 | 43 → 43 |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-Q4_0 | 204 → 205 | 268 → 454 | 419 → 718 | 871 → 942 | 117 → 115 |

Kernels by @fernando-neto-ai, developed on Liquid AI's fork. This PR keeps the stock crossover thresholds; the fork's retuned (M3-measured) values were slightly slower on M4.

### Name and Version

```
% ./llama-cli --version
version: 10326 (ceebfc910)
built with Clang 22.1.8 for Linux x86_64
```

(Rebase of #26692. Happening on multiple builds made after 1269cb1f (most likely also earlier), the last commit touching `src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.*`, `src/models/deepseek4.cpp`, or `src/llama-batch.cpp`.)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

9950X + RTX 6000

### Models

unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF, UD-IQ1_S, UD-IQ2_M

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When deepseek4 runs with both `-np` > 1 and speculation enabled, the model will eventually start producing nonsense output. Both options must be enabled at once for this to happen. If the speculation is disabled, inference works correctly with multiple parallel generations. If only one slot is enabled, the model works correctly with speculation enabled (i.e., dspark, confirmed enabled by 2x tg speed).

---

Fable 5 analysis of the issue:

> TLDR: I found a real, code-verified bug that matches your symptoms exactly — but it only fires when speculative decoding (MTP/DSpark) is enabled alongside -np 2. If you're running with --spec-type mtp (or a draft sidecar), this is almost certainly your bug. Nothing else in the multi-sequence path survived the audit as a suspect.
> 
> The bug: rollback restore is replayed across ubatches, poisoning the compressed KV caches
> 
> DeepSeek-V4's sparse attention keeps, per sequence, a small ring of "compressor state" rows plus rollback snapshot planes (used to undo rejected speculative drafts). The bug is in how the per-ubatch graph plans are built:
> 
> - llama_kv_cache_dsv4_context's constructor (src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.cpp:1993-2001) builds the compressor plans for all ubatches of a batch up front, from a single snapshot of the pending-rollback array rs_idx. The array is reset only after all plans exist (:2028).
> - Each plan emits a "restore plane[rollback] → plane[0]" copy for every sequence it contains (:624-638), executed at the start of every ubatch's graph.
> 
> With -np 2 the DSv4 cache forces split_equal ubatch splitting, which expands the two sequences in lockstep and stops as soon as the shorter one runs out (src/llama-batch.cpp:573-603). So whenever your two slots contribute unequal token counts to one llama_decode — different accepted-draft lengths, or one slot decoding while the other processes a prompt chunk — the longer sequence spans two ubatches. Ubatch A applies the rollback correctly and advances the ring state; ubatch B then re-applies the same rollback, reverting ring rows that ubatch A just wrote. Every compressed block committed afterward whose window reaches back across the ubatch boundary is computed from stale rows and written permanently into the CSA/HCA caches and — worse — the lightning-indexer key cache.
> 
> That's why the failure looks the way it does: the raw sliding-window cache is untouched, so short-range attention is exact and the text stays locally coherent. What rots is long-range recall (compressed keys) and the indexer's top-k selection (which keys get attended at all) — "seemingly coherent but in the long run not what it should be." Tool calling is hit hardest for two reasons: it depends on exact long-range recall of tool schemas, and the multi-turn tool flow (prompt-cache reuse trimming the parsed tail, partial draft accepts) is precisely what arms rollbacks on every step.
> 
> Why -np 1 is clean: a single sequence's batch fits in one ubatch, so the restore runs exactly once. Why quantization/CUDA don't matter: the bug is index-plan logic in src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.cpp, backend-agnostic.
> 
> Without speculation, none of this machinery runs (n_rs_seq == 0 skips restore planning entirely, and partial seq_rm is refused at :1427), so the bug needs both -np 2 and MTP/DSpark/DFlash/EAGLE3 enabled.
> 
> How to confirm on your machine
> 
> 1. Run your -np 2 setup with speculation disabled (drop --spec-type / draft sidecar). If the degradation disappears while -np 2 stays on, it's confirmed.
> 2. LLAMA_DSV4_COMPRESS_DEBUG=1 logs the plan contents if you want to watch the replayed restores.
> 3. If you were not running speculation at all, tell me — then this bug doesn't apply and the main remaining mundane suspect is that -np 2 halves the per-slot context (n_ctx_seq in the startup log), which produces a similar "coherent but wrong, tool calls break" signature when conversations outgrow it.
> 
> What was ruled out
> 
> I ran a deep three-way audit (custom DSv4 KV cache, graph-input/mask filling, CUDA kernels). Verified correct, stride-by-stride against the CPU reference where relevant: the fused CUDA lightning-indexer and hyper-connection kernels with 2 streams, top-k/set-rows mask scatter, per-stream mask filling and offsets, graph-reuse guards, and the multi-stream K-write paths. Two benign side findings: a harmless head-restore mis-index at src/llama-kv-cache.cpp:802 (v_heads_old[s] should be v_heads_old[sinfo.strm[s]] — allocation-locality only), and there's currently no flag to disable the fused DSv4 ops for A/B testing.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

```
[DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731]
model = /home/wolf/Models/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF/UD-IQ1_S/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-IQ1_S-00001-of-00003.gguf
model-draft = /home/wolf/Models/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf
spec-type = draft-dspark
spec-draft-n-max = 3

ctx-size = 1000000

items.body:
common_base_params_to_speculative copies the target's n_batch/n_ubatch into the draft params and never reduces them. The draft context then sizes its compute buffers for the target's batch (4096 here) even though the same function computes that a block drafter emits only n_max + 1 tokens.

For a small drafter this waste is negligible, which is what the existing comment above assumes. A DFlash/DSpark drafter is an MoE model - 3 blocks of 256 experts - so the oversized buffers cost 4-6 GB: a 7.2 GB Q2_K drafter held 11-13 GB resident.

On a 64 GB M1 Max that memory comes out of the MoE expert cache. Before this, DeepSeek-V4-Flash at --moe-stream-cache 38 plus the drafter thrashed (1.2 GB swap, prefill timed out); after, prefill is 86.3 t/s and the config runs.

Safe because drafting submits n_seq*(n_max+1) tokens - at most 17 for any supported block size - and prompt processing already chunks by n_ubatch in common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash::process().

items.body:
## Summary

The official LiquidAI LFM2.5-2.6B DSpark GGUF sidecar loads successfully, but llama-server crashes on the first generation request with a native graph assertion on macOS Apple Silicon.

## Environment

- OS: macOS on Apple Silicon
- llama.cpp: Homebrew build 10470
- Target: LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF, LFM2.5-2.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf
- Draft sidecar: official LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-DSpark-GGUF, LFM2.5-2.6B-DSpark-F16.gguf
- Official sidecar model card: https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-DSpark-GGUF

## Reproduction

Start:

```bash
llama-server \
  -m LFM2.5-2.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -md LFM2.5-2.6B-DSpark-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dspark \
  --spec-draft-n-max 9 \
  --spec-draft-n-min 0 \
  -ngl 99 \
  --jinja \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8083 \
  -c 4096
```

The server reports that the model loaded and DSpark was initialized:

```text
adding speculative implementation 'draft-dspark'
- n_max=9, n_min=0, p_min=0.00
- block_size=9, mask_token_id=125017, n_extract=5, sample_from_anchor=true
model loaded
listening on http://127.0.0.1:8083
```

Send:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8083/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"LFM2.5-2.6B-Q4_K_M","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello."}],"max_tokens":16,"temperature":0}'
```

Observed result: the client receives an empty reply and the server exits.

Relevant crash:

```text
src/llama-graph.cpp:1352: GGML_ASSERT(t_layer_inp[il] != nullptr && "layer input tensor is null") failed
```

The same crash occurs with a 32768-token context and with flash attention disabled. The non-DSpark router using the same target GGUF continues to work normally.

## Expected behavior

The request should complete successfully with DSpark speculative decoding, or llama-server should return a clear compatibility error instead of aborting via a native assertion.

## This has been closed with plans to organize and re-open
I have redesigned about half of the entire system in ways that fix all major issues exposed by this pr. I have not decided yet if ill push here or make a new clean pr with a new commit history after applying the final changes one by one. I still have some work but this is just a heads up that I am aware of the issues and im fixing them
## Overview

I want to make this as short as possible. I made a CUDA only for now feature where it tracks a heat map of all expert usage and the hottest experts are cached on GPU and computed there, while cold experts are computed on the CPU. off by default can be set by "--expert-hot-s N" (or -ehs for short), autofit from free VRAM using the native auto fit functions sizing based on how many experts would be offset to the cpu "--expert-hot-s -1", or off (0, default). But if you want to test you an use --ecf to force it on

Also adds: hysteresis gate + dwell on slot swaps, per-expert scale handling, a CUDA-only backend guard (Vulkan/CPU are rejected with a warning as I have not managed to get non cuda gpus to work fully and honestly can't figure it out and it does nothing on a cpu install, but still left a force activate argument), and auto-activation of --cmoe when manual slots are selected as the GPU will act as caching not slots.

Measured on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_M / Q5_K_P with 8 GB VRAM: ~1.7-2.1x
steady-state decode speedup over stock (56 vs 33 tok/s, 36 vs 17 tok/s) using autofit.

## Additional information

Known limitations:
- Tier only engages at n_tokens == 1 (single-token decode); multi-slotbatches fall back to stock mul_mat_id.
- Verified on separate gate/up expert tensors (Qwen-style). Gemma 4 seemed broken as it resulted in incoherent output and initially i theorized it was because of `gate_up_exps` models breaking my implementation. but aparently the model i tried to run had stopped working on the latest upstream too, even tho it works fine on the one from a few days ago. So does not seem like my issue. I am almost certain it works properly, but i would appreciate a correction
- CUDA-only by design; the guard logs a warning and skips the tier on other back-ends unless forcefully activated.
- Due to differences in how experts are processed on the CPU vs the GPU, even at temp 0 when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
- Not intended for multiple GPUs. Aparently it CAN work but I have no way of testing and developing it currently.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: Yes. On most the steps I got stuck I brainstormed with AI on how to resolve each problem, although all final code was written or verified by me (Although note i am not heavily experienced). Ai also caught and corrected a few of the smaller bugs in my code or changes the defaults/names of variables when i could not be bothered to do it manually.

Some numbers have been updated to reflect the minor optimization I commited. The full optimization numbers are better, but I wont put them here till its ready as thats misleading

Original llama.cpp vs my pull request
| Model | Size | S | Stock (tok/s) | Request (tok/s) | Ratio | Coherent after 128k tokens? |

### Research Stage

- [x] Background Research (Let's try to avoid reinventing the wheel)
- [x] Hypothesis Formed (How do you think this will work and it's effect?)
- [x] Strategy / Implementation Forming
- [ ] Analysis of results
- [ ] Debrief / Documentation (So people in the future can learn from us)

### Previous existing literature and research

[https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02123](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02123)

The paper claims: `(...) measured speedup gains over autoregressive (AR) decoding, relative to matched DSpark, range from 3.1% to 29.5%. `

I chatted with an LLM about the implementation of DSpark and I wondered why we arent utilizing multiple paths from the markov head at once.
It then pointed me directly to this fairly recent paper which execises exactly this topic, 

In the PC tree approach they describe, they reuse DSparks normal (single linear speculative) approach and markov head, but use multiple "parent conditioned continuations", meaning they "branch off" in parallel.

With reusing dspark, we would in theory just need to change some code and not retrain anything (given a dspark model exists for a model).



### Hypothesis

Since DSpark is already computing the shared block prediction, we can just use the "cheap" markov head predictions on different parent tokens.
A tree may contain another branch whose continuatioon matches the target farther ahead.

E.g: Should lead to faster overall generation throughput per target verification round, given the tree verification overhead remains low enough.
Obviously too many parallel branches will lead to a reduction (similar how MTP or such behaves in effect).
Also what is a given, is that VRAM must increase marginially in order to hold those parallel branches with their drafts each (KV).

It could also be that parallelism here plain just doesnt perform better, because the branching itself costs some time (latency). 
The paper stated this:

```
B = speculative block/depth budget
k = frontier width
N = verifier node budget

For Qwen3-4B, k=4, N=32:

B=7
DSpark Markov: 0.65 ms/round
PCTree Markov+tree: 3.52 ms/round
so the tree adds about +2.87 ms/round

B=16
DSpark Markov: 1.09 ms/round
PCTree Markov+tree: 5.24 ms/round
so about +4.15 ms/round
```
but in their speed in general improved:
```
B=7:   4.24x -> 4.50x
B=16:  6.14x -> 6.60x
```
Therefore the PC Tree was still worth it, even with the compute time penalty.

### Implementation

Im currently working on implementing and testing this approach (with the help of multiple LLMs):

[getraid/llama.cpp-dspark-pctree](https://github.com/getraid/llama.cpp-dspark-pctree)

this is not fully functional yet, prolly has a bunch of mistakes and incompatablites and currently at the time of writing perfoms slower than any other already working approach. But its integrated for both CPU and CUDA currently. 
I will continue with testing, writing and verifying it and update this issue/research accordingly.

If you guys think this fits the "vibe"/approach of llamacpp, i will clean up the the implementation and submit a PR (or multiple with CPU first, then CUDA, etc) afterwards. Just let me know.

Also if someone else wants to also tackle this approach and beat me to it: feel free :)

### Analysis
* The "swings" you normally have with the generation are amplified. Meaning if you use dspark and the model drafts, verifies and generates between 70-110tps it now gets more drastic with up to 180tps for example, but will avg around ~140 tps. 
   * So improvement in general, but wide "swings".

TBD. I have some conclusions already, but i need further testing.

## Overview

This change assigns a static workspace buffer per-device for cublas, allocating the nvidia recommended workspace size according to the device arch.

You will also notice that cublas handle usage has been slightly adjusted so that we automatically set the workspace after every SetStream, because according to nvidia docs: "The cublasSetStream() function unconditionally resets the cuBLAS library workspace back to the default workspace pool" (I'm not sure why nvidia set it up to behave this way, but that's how it works)

This is an attempt to address the issues found in #26119 and probably also #26554, which would have both been affected by my change in #25749. There seems to be a correlation between these crashes and Volta/Turing + graphs, but reading through the docs I'm unsure why it wouldn't effect other archs, maybe the dynamic workspace allocation works differently on these older archs?

Changes are primarily based on information from: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html#cublassetworkspace

## Additional information

Anecdotally, I haven't had issues running this branch for a few days, and the user from #26119 says that this patch fixed the crash they were seeing.

Also, I saw no apparent performance changes

## Overview

In `build_attn` for the `llm_graph_input_attn_k_iswa` input (MLA-style attention where the cached K is used as V), V was the cached K tensor itself. It is now created as a view of K (the first `v_cur->ne[0]` elements of each row), like the other K-only `build_attn` overloads (`llm_graph_input_attn_k`, `llm_graph_input_attn_k_dsa`).

All current callers (deepseek4 MTP block, dflash DSpark decoder) have equal K/V head sizes, so the view is full-size and the attention results are unchanged — V simply becomes a proper view of K, which lets backends detect the V-is-view-of-K pattern.

The deepseek4 MTP call site now passes the `kv` tensor as `v_cur` (it passed `nullptr` before).

## Additional information

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27390 (Metal FA: skip the redundant V dequant when V is a view of K)

### Summary

With DSpark speculative decoding (`--spec-type draft-dspark`) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, llama-server reliably aborts with a CUDA error after roughly **2,000–2,600 decoded tokens** in a single response. Three crashes over two days, all with the same signature; short responses never crash. Reproduced on **b10242 and b10257**.

### Error

```
/home/mp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:106: CUDA error
E CUDA error: an unsupported value or parameter was passed to the function
E   current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_mul_mat_cublas_impl at /home/mp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:1541
E   cublasSgemm_v2(ctx.cublas_handle(), CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, ne01, ne11, ne10, (const float *) alpha, (const float *) src0_ptr, s01, (const float *) src1_ptr, s11, (const float *) beta, (float *) dst_ptr, ne0)
```

Last server log line before the abort (crash #3):

```
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 7 | n_decoded =   2518, tg =  20.42 t/s, tg_3s =  21.22 t/s
```

### Pattern

| Crash | Build | Prompt tokens | Decoded before abort | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #1 | b10242 | ~11k | ~2,5–3k (est., 16.6 t/s × ~3 min) | long reasoning response |
| #2 | b10242 | ~4k | ~2–2.5k (est.) | long reasoning response |
| #3 | b10257 | ~4k | **2,518** (from `print_timing`) | long reasoning response |

- Only long, reasoning-heavy generations crash; code-heavy answers of a few hundred tokens are fine.
- An FP32 GEMM (`cublasSgemm_v2`) in the decode path looks unusual — suspicion: the DSpark markov head or the DeepSeek sparse-attention indexer produces a degenerate shape (a dim/stride of 0 or an ld below the cuBLAS minimum) once the sequence crosses some threshold.
- For comparison: Qwen MTP profiles (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`, same machine, same multi-GPU setup) have never shown this crash. We are currently testing whether `--spec-draft-n-max 3` instead of 5 avoids it on DSpark, too.

### Setup

- Model: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` UD-Q4_K_XL (unsloth GGUF, 5 split files) + `dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf` sidecar
- GPUs: 2× Quadro RTX 8000 (48 GB) + 3× Tesla V100-PCIE-32GB, pinned via `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<uuid list>` (RTX first)
- Driver 580.173.02, CUDA runtime 13.0, built with nvcc 12.0, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70;75`, Linux x86_64
- Command (crash #3, `${PORT}` filled in by llama-swap):

```
llama-server --port ${PORT} \
  --model .../DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00005.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -c 137728 -sm layer --tensor-split 12,12,6,8,5 -fit off \
  -b 2048 -ub 2048 --flash-attn on -np 1 -t 4 --mlock --direct-io \
  --jinja --reasoning-format deepseek --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-k 40 --top-p 1.0 --min-p 0.05 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  --model-draft .../dspark/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 5 --gpu-layers-draft 99 \
  --device-draft CUDA4 --cache-reuse 256
```

(K/V cache f16; the draft sidecar is pinned to the device holding the main model's output layer — other placements abort at load with `pre-allocated tensor (output.weight) in a buffer (CUDA4) that cannot run the operation`.)

Happy to provide full logs, GDB backtraces or test patches — the crash is reproducible within minutes by asking for a long reasoning answer.

3653e6d6d

Replacing only the remote ROCm RPC worker with a Vulkan/RADV RPC worker on the exact same Radeon 8060S / gfx1151 hardware makes the same setup stable.

Vulkan is significantly slower, but it does not crash.

This appears related to #24177 because both failures involve the AMD `TOP_K` path and an RPC worker abort.

1. Start a ROCm `ggml-rpc-server` on the gfx1151 remote system.
2. Start `llama-server` with the command above.
3. Send a short chat request.

## How to run

Complete example from scratch (gemma-4-12B-it).

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --local-dir Gemma4-12B-it
hf download deepseek-ai/dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --local-dir dspark_gemma4_12b_block7

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Gemma4-12B-it --outtype bf16 --outfile Gemma4-12B-it.gguf

  --outfile Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf

You may quantize the *target*; keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j

items.body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> Off-topic comments and AI slop/spam in this thread will be deleted. Keep the discussion focused.

---

Draft. Adds support for `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` (HF `model_type: qwen4_exp`, `Qwen4ExpForConditionalGeneration`): converter, text graph, sparse attention, vision, and three quantizer fixes the model needs. Opening as a draft because the weights are not public yet, so the accuracy numbers below cannot be reproduced from outside at the moment.

## Architecture

| subsystem | how it is handled |
|---|---|
| Gated delta net (3 of every 4 layers) | subclasses the existing delta-net base; the only delta from Qwen3.5 is a sigmoid output gate instead of silu |
| MoE, 512 experts, top-10, gated shared expert | `build_moe_ffn`, unchanged |
| Interleaved mrope, partial rotary 64/256 | `ggml_rope_multi` with `LLAMA_ROPE_TYPE_IMROPE`, unchanged |
| Hyper-connections (`hc_count = 4`, low rank) | self-contained in `qwen4exp.cpp`; `deepseek4.cpp` is untouched |
| Per-layer embeddings, 97.7 GiB n-gram hash table | host-side row indices in a `set_input`, then `ggml_get_rows` |
| QSA sparse attention (budget 2048, ratio 4) | new graph plus an optional third cache in `llama_memory_hybrid` |
| Vision | stock Qwen3-VL ViT through the existing clip path |

`git diff master --stat -- ggml/` is empty: no new ggml op, and no change to any existing one.

## Correctness, against the reference implementation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| wikitext-2 perplexity, 145 chunks at ctx 2048 | 4.0068 +/- 0.02271 vs 4.0126 for the reference |
| top-1 agreement, 512 tokens of prose | 98.0 percent |
| QSA vs dense below the budget | bit identical, max logit delta 0.0 over all 2051 rows |
| QSA vs dense above the budget, 8192 tokens | diverges on 3 percent of positions |
| indexer selection vs the reference | 0.975 mean jaccard against a 0.991 precision floor |
| `test-llama-archs -a qwen4exp` | OK on CPU (0.00e+00) and CUDA (8.00e-08), roundtrip OK |

The bit-identical result below the budget is the useful one: QSA is dense by construction under `indexer_top_k + compress_ratio - 1` cached tokens, so it is a free oracle on the whole selection and masking path.

## Effect on other architectures

Six shared files contain deletions rather than pure additions:

- `llama-quant.cpp`: three fixes, each byte-exact against the parent commit. `tensor_type_fallback` had no case for 32-block types, so a tensor whose ncols is not divisible by 32 aborted instead of falling back; `--tensor-type` could not name `per_layer_token_embd` because `--token-embedding-type` returned first; and the `work` buffer was sized `nelements * 4` as an upper bound on a value already known exactly, which is 150 GB per process on a model with a 51.2 G element tensor. Six A/B cases, six matching md5s.
- `llama-graph.cpp`: `build_attn_mask_top_k` lifted verbatim out of the DSA `build_attn` overload so both share it. The node construction sequence is identical after splicing the helper back into its call site, and `deepseek32` and `glm-dsa` both pass at 0.00e+00 on CPU.
- `llama-memory-hybrid.cpp`: the new `filter_idx` defaults to `nullptr` and every use is guarded.
- `llama-model-loader.cpp`: adds a `GGUF_TYPE_UINT64` case to a type check that previously threw.
- `llama-hparams.cpp`, `llama-model.cpp`: new fields and new switch cases.

A shared hyper-connection base with `deepseek4` was considered and rejected: the two formulations agree on the residual layout and nothing else (full-rank projection with Sinkhorn normalisation there, low-rank silu gate and a mean collapse here), so factoring it out would touch DSV4's hot path to share about ten lines.

## Note for reviewers

This branch was developed against a snapshot and rebased onto current master. Two rebase conflicts were resolved by hand, both additive: `test-llama-archs.cpp` where master had added a `LLM_ARCH_DEEPSEEK4` condition to a line this port also edits, and `llama-model-saver.cpp` where master reworked the DSV4 key block. Worth a close look, since the local build was against the pre-rebase tree.

## AI Usage

## Overview

Kind of a big overhaul of the Hexagon backend to enable support for mulit-NPU devices, and to make it fully asynchronous: async graph-compute, async events, async tensor-copy, cross-device fences -- the whole enchilada!

The PR also includes everything required to properly support and enable multi-NPU tensor-split mode (ie integration with the meta backend) on devices like the [IQ9](https://www.qualcomm.com/internet-of-things/products/iq9-series) and [IQ10](https://www.qualcomm.com/internet-of-things/products/iq10-series) series. 
Tested on the [IQ9 EVK](https://www.qualcomm.com/developer/hardware/qualcomm-iq-9075-evaluation-kit-evk).
See examples below.

The asynchronous implementation ended up requiring many other updates besides just making `graph_compute` and `cpy_tensor_async` not block. To make it fully usable we need to use non-host buffers by default (ie to force async copies and repack), which in turn requires support for more types in `SET/GET_ROWS`, etc. The CPY op needed to be optimized to not slow things down, and to support fused FENCE op to allow for truly async copies.
Hence this PR includes all those updates.  

The multi-NPU support requires new device naming scheme. The original naming `HTP0,...HTP4` is still supported and is enabled if the environment variable `GGML_HEXAGON_NDEV` is defined.  The new scheme is `HTP0:0, HTP1:0` where the first number is physical NPU id and the second number is the virtual id of the session. 

To simplify the migration and support for the devices I included new `./scripts/snapdragon/build.py` and `./scripts/snapdragon/run.py`  and update the documenation to cover the new scripts, devices, etc.

## Additional information

Here is an example gemma-4-E4B (q4_0 QAT model) on IQ9 EVK in tensor split mode

```
./scripts/snapdragon/run.py --target ubuntu:maxk@192.168.1.87 --device HTP0:0,HTP1:0 -- llama-completion \
     -m gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf -f sample_prompt_1024.txt --jinja -st --split-mode tensor --ctx-size 8192
```

## Overview

Long-context generation quickly exhausts VRAM when retaining the entire KV cache. This PR implements StreamingLLM-style KV cache eviction via `--kv-evict-sink` and `--kv-evict-window`.

By capping the physical cache at `sink + recent + n_ubatch` cells while allowing the logical context to grow indefinitely, both VRAM footprint and per-token decode latency remain constant over arbitrary sequence lengths.

## Implementation Details

- **Masking**: `set_input_kq_mask_impl` masks cells in the range `[n_kv_sink, p1 - n_kv_recent)`. Mask row reuse is disabled while eviction is active.

- **Slot Recycling**: `find_slot` reclaims the oldest cell outside the sink and active recent window; `apply_ubatch` bypasses contiguity purges during eviction.

- **Memory Footprint**: Fixed at `n_seq_max * (sink + recent) + ubatch` for unified multi-sequence caches (`sink + recent + ubatch` otherwise). Recurrent states (e.g., DeltaNet) remain untouched.

- **Compatibility**: Disables context shifting (`get_can_shift = false`). Safe for MTP speculative decoding since rollback spans stay within the recent window.

- **Benchmarks**: Wikitext-2 perplexity remains stable (~6.31 baseline vs. ~6.48 with a 1024-token window), while decode throughput stays flat across long sequences.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

- AI Usage disclosure: YES - the code implementation was drafted with AI and reviewed/tested by me before submission.

## Overview

DFlash2 adds two more modules compared to DFlash, grouped dynamic depthwise convolution and candidate selector. 

The formula is for reference. `out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c]`. `base` is the static kernel, `δ` is the dynamic part predicted from the input.`x` is divided into groups `g(c)` and `δ` is shared across a group. Another one is `edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c]`. `A`/`B` are the codebooks for the predecessor and the candidate. This position's hidden is projected by `project(h)`to the same rank to multiply `A`. And `unary[c]` is the draft's own score for `c`.  

DFlash2 is enabled when the checkpoint is DFlash2; no need to use extra flag.

We evaled `Qwen3.8-27B` at `Q4_K_M`on Apple M5 Pro 64 GB. And the test data is first 8 problems of GSM8K.
Concurrency is set to 1 and temperature is 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20. We use default `xhigh` reasoning and set
2,048 maximum new tokens.

|--------|------|--:|------:|------:|-----:|---|
| Autoregressive | — | — | 10.42 | 1.00× | — | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | BF16 | 8 | 19.31 | 1.85× | 4.92 | 8/8 |

## Overview Follow‑up to #26373, address the feedback in PR-26373. **Qualcomm’s Hexagon SDK provides two RPC mechanisms**: native FastRPC and dspqueue. this PR adds **FastRPC-based ggml-hexagon**, an alternative backend for Qualcomm Hexagon NPU on Android & WoA(Windows on Snapdragon), which can coexist with **the existing dspqueue-based** ggml-hexagon implementation. This relationship is similar to ggml‑openvino vs ggml‑sycl (backends for the same hardware), or ggml‑cuda vs ggml‑hip (ggml‑hip reuses existing CUDA kernels) within llama.cpp. ## Big changes compared to PR‑26373 - remove **redundant AP‑side** cache coherency maintenance, allowing the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon to work on WoA devices - 100% reuse of existing Hexagon kernels - reuse the existing build system from the dspqueue‑based ggml‑hexagon - refine ggmlhexagon_init_rpcmempool, so the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon **should** work fine on Snapdragon 8 Elite 5(aka 8Gen5) phones. ## Features 1. single shared mempool + Native FastRPC: lm-head offloading is the primary factor behind the drastic PP and TG throughput advantage seen in this PR, lm‑head offloading is heavily dependent on the single shared mempool design. 2. role-aware cache coherency in **NPU-side**: it distinguishes resident weights from per-batch activations and applies first-touch cache invalidation only once for resident weights. 3. minimal code footprint & coexistence: the fastrpc backend introduces minimal code footprint, can **directly 100% re-use the existing hexagon kernels** and the two backends share one HTP ops source tree (htp/), only a handful of files are truly new or modified. the two backends are **build-time variants of one backend directory and one build system**, selected by a single option: `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` plus `GGML_HEXAGON_USE_MEMPOOL=ON` builds the fastrpc backend (`ggml-hexagon-fastrpc.cpp` + `htp/entry.c` + `htp/ggml_htp.idl`); `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` alone (default) builds the dspqueue backend (`ggml-hexagon.cpp` + `htp/main.c` + `htp/htp_iface.idl`), exactly the upstream behavior. ## Overview

Issue #27194
- Fuses UNARY(GELU|SIGMOID|SILU|SOFTPLUS)+MUL on Vulkan, matching CUDA's unary_mul
- Review-driven additions:
  - GELU support (gemma4/gemma3n per-layer gating)
  - shape check via standard `ggml_can_repeat`
  - fusion of pairs separated by zero-compute nodes (graph_optimize)
  - OP-on-B support (`ffn_shexp * sigmoid(gate)`, qwen3next/qwen35moe shared-expert gating)

## Additional information

### Design:
- Fusion lives in unary.comp behind UNARY_MUL_FUSION. Specialized pipelines per
  op/dtype, repeat + norepeat variants selected by shape equality. Kernel
  scheduled like mul.comp (256 threads x 2 iterations); writes the MUL dst
  directly, never materializing the unary intermediate.
- Shape gating uses the standard `ggml_can_repeat` broadcast check (admits non-1
  repeat factors, matching ggml and CUDA reference semantics).
- Both operand slots supported:
  - unary as src0: other must repeat against it (`ggml_can_repeat(other, unary)`)
  - unary as src1 (OP-on-B, e.g. qwen shared-expert gating `ffn_shexp * sigmoid(gate)`):
    the unary result must tile into mul->src[0]; a UNARY_MUL_B variant iterates over
    mul's extent and applies the OP to the fastmod-indexed B operand. A backend-local
    pair check (`ggml_can_fuse_subgraph` + Vulkan shape rules) replaces the generic
    same-shape requirement of `ggml_can_fuse` for this pattern. The OP-on-B choice is
    a `op_on_b` specialization constant on the *existing* unary-mul SPIR-V — no
    separate _mul_b shaders — selected via two-entry `{norepeat, op_on_b}` lists,
    mirroring how `norepeat` already works.
- graph_optimize: a consuming MUL may now join its in-set UNARY across a gap of
  unscheduled zero-compute nodes (NONE/VIEW/RESHAPE/TRANSPOSE/PERMUTE). The
  mechanism is a scoped strict-adjacency extension of the existing UNARY->MUL
  blessed pair; in practice GEMMA-3n's per-layer views fall into an earlier
  window's scan range and land ahead of the UNARY, after which strict adjacency
  suffices. Pipelines are stored in a lookup table
  `pipeline_unary_mul[4][2][2][2]` ([op][f16][norepeat][op_on_b]) replacing the
  four nested selection switches.

### Tests:
- Fused ops: 104/104 layouts
  (packed/padded/halves/broadcast/non-1-repeat/view-separated/OP-on-B gate gate
   x gelu/sigmoid/silu/softplus x f32/f16)
- Plain ops: MUL 91/91
- 16957 tests, all backends OK (up from 16935 at the time of the original PR).
- Dispatch-path verified on debug builds (grep `*_mul_f32/_mul_b_f32` descriptor
  requests) and via the sched-driven probe covering adjacent, view-separated,
  reshape-separated, and OP-on-B-broadcast graphs.
- Token-identical vs base build (`4df29be4f`) at temp 0 / seed 42 on Qwen3-8B,
  Gemma-3n-E4B, gemma4-12B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B.
- Hardware: AMD Radeon 8050S Graphics (RADV STRIX_HALO), uma.

./build/bin/test-backend-ops -b Vulkan0 -o MUL            # 91/91 OK

Fixes crash when running with Gemma MTP and Tensor. Originally found while playing with [beelama](https://github.com/Anbeeld/beellama.cpp), discovered it also affected mainline, and found others with the issue. 

Two contexts sharing memory under SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR (e.g. Gemma4 MTP or EAGLE3 draft + target) both create views into the same meta-backend buffers. Reusing a stale graph after the peer has rebuilt leaves dangling per-device tensor references, causing fattn.cu:579 crashes.

Fix: disable graph reuse for both contexts when either uses tensor split and they share memory. Backend-agnostic, applies to Gemma4 MTP and EAGLE3. 

Confirmed on 2x 7900 XTX (ROCm/HIP/RCCL) with 3 sequential same-slot requests.
Also confirmed on NVIDIA by testers in #24314.

Fixes #24324, #24314, #24440

items.body:
This patch implements the event and async APIs from the backend interface. The intent is to enable pipeline parallelism with the RPC backend.

Here is a summary of the changes:
 * Introduce `rpc_dispatcher` which allows sending commands both synchronously and asynchronously to an RPC endpoint. There is one dispatcher per RPC endpoint and every dispatcher is using a background thread for its network communication.
 * All RPC commands are allocated on the heap and passed to `rpc_dispatcher` with `shared_ptr`s to avoid making copies of the input data.
 * Creating an event adds a dummy message in the dispatcher's queue and synchronizing the event waits for this dummy message to be processed by the background thread. Not sure if this is equivalent to how CUDA events work which seem to be the inspiration of the backend API.
 * Changed `RPC_CMD_FREE_BUFFER`, `RPC_CMD_BUFFER_CLEAR`, `RPC_CMD_INIT_TENSOR` to not send any response which simplifies the logic in the dispatcher. Hence the protocol version bump (3.7.0).

TODO:
 * Verify event implementation; Are `event_synchronize()` and `event_wait()` equivalent here?
 * Implement `cpy_tensor_async()`. This is a hard one as RPC servers need to to talk to each other (see PR #8032). Pipeline parallelism relies on both `graph_compute()` and `cpy_tensor_async()` being async and I am not sure if we are going to see improvements only with the former.
 * Split RPC backend into several files (e.g. client, server, common). This is left for a future refactoring PR with no functional changes.

@ggerganov I will appreciate some early feedback on this.

## Overview

**Co-authors:** @jxia4intel, @sliu39

**PR 2/3** of the Intel Xe optimization series — see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24408 (mega PR, draft) for the full feature set.

**Target platforms:** Xe-LPG Plus, Xe2, Xe3

This PR adds Intel Xe-specific flash attention optimization kernels for both ARLH iGPU (Xe1, UMA, coopmat1) and Xe2/Xe3. Dependency: builds on top of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24404 (Xe-LPG Plus coopmat1 enable). Independent of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24407 (GEMM+CW).

### Flash Attention (Intel Xe)

- New Vulkan shaders: single-phase prefill (`flash_attn_hdim64/96/128`) and two-phase split prefill/decode variants
- Pipelines keyed by `(head_dim, gqa_ratio)` for runtime dispatch across various GQA ratios without combinatorial pipeline proliferation
- Supports non-power-of-two GQA ratios via subgroup splitting (`qk_groups`)
- Intel Xe1 (integrated GPU, UMA, cooperative matrix) and Xe2 paths with separate warptile tuning
- Two-phase decode splits softmax reduction across subgroups; shared QK state copy (`fa_copy_qstate`) between prefill phases

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

### Name and Version build : b10549-b2e5e9b28 windows vulkan 64bit ### Operating systems Windows ### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected? llama-server ### Command line ```shell Server (no speedup from MTP): llama-server.exe ^ -m "Gemma4-26B-A4B-QAT-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Balanced.Q4_0.gguf" ^ --model-draft "mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf" ^ --spec-type draft-mtp ^ --spec-draft-n-max 2 ^ -np 1 ^ -ngl 99 ^ -c 34096 ^ -b 512 ^ --mlock ^ --flash-attn on ^ --no-mmap ^ --temp 0.6 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.9 --min-p 0.05 --repeat-penalty 1.1 ^ --jinja ^ --chat-template-file "chat_template.jinja" ^ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8081 --ctx-size 34096 CLI (full MTP speedup, same models/params): llama-cli.exe ^ -m "Gemma4-26B-A4B-QAT-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Balanced.Q4_0.gguf" ^ --model-draft "mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf" ^ --spec-type draft-mtp ^ --spec-draft-n-max 2 ^ -ngl 99 -c 34096 -b 512 ^ --mlock --flash-attn on --no-mmap ^ --temp 0.6 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.9 --min-p 0.05 --repeat-penalty 1.1 ^ --jinja ^ --chat-template-file "chat_template.jinja" ^ ``` ### Problem description & steps to reproduce This is in regard to core ultra 135u igpu with unified memory.

Problem description & steps to reproduce

With MTP speculative decoding enabled, llama-cli gets a consistent, repeatable ~25–30% generation speedup over the plain (non-MTP) baseline. llama-server, run with the identical model pair and identical sampling/context/GPU-offload flags, gets effectively no speedup from MTP — despite a healthy draft acceptance rate (draft tokens are being accepted, not rejected).

Baseline (MTP flags removed entirely) is identical between the two binaries, which rules out generic server/CLI dispatch overhead as the cause and isolates the regression to the MTP draft/verify path specifically:

  | No MTP | With MTP (--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2) -- | -- | -- llama-cli | 6.8 t/s | ~8.5–9.2 t/s llama-server | 6.8 t/s | ~6.7–6.8 t/s

Server-side draft acceptance is reported as healthy (see log below), so the draft model is doing useful work — the accepted tokens simply aren't translating into wall-clock throughput on the server the way they do on the CLI.

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Launch llama-server with the command above.
  2. Send a single completion/chat request with a long-form prompt (~1800+ generated tokens in my testing) and note timings.predicted_per_second and the draft acceptance line in the server console.
  3. Launch llama-cli with the equivalent command (same models, same sampling params, -p/-n instead of a server request) and note the [ Prompt: X t/s | Generation: Y t/s ] summary.
  4. Repeat both with --model-draft/--spec-type/--spec-draft-n-max removed entirely to get the non-MTP baseline for each.
  5. Compare: baseline matches within noise; MTP uplift does not.
(CLI on this build does not print the detailed n_draft/n_accept breakdown even at -lv 2; only the summary line above is available — happy to rebuild with a patch or test flag if that would help narrow this down further.) Additional notes Both binaries give identical throughput (6.8 t/s) with MTP disabled, so this does not appear to be generic server dispatch/slot-loop overhead — it's specific to how the server executes the draft/verify cycle. Not immediately fixed by upstream PR #17808 ("server: improve speed of speculative decoding") — my build (b10549-b2e5e9b28) postdates that merge by a wide margin. Possibly related, though none is an exact match for this combination (Vulkan, discrete GPU, llama-server, healthy acceptance rate, zero net speedup): #23126 — Vulkan UMA/iGPU draft+target serialization (my case may or may not be UMA; symptom matches, hardware class may not) #23752 — MTP net-negative/net-zero throughput on Metal despite good acceptance (symptom matches closely, different backend) #27428 — draft-mtp regression on multi-GPU layer splits; code discussion explicitly references Gemma 4's MTP mem-share path in common/speculative.cpp, though the reported trigger there is layer-split specific and my setup is single-GPU ### First Bad Commit _No response_ ### Relevant log output slot print_timing: id 0 | task 0 | eval time = 258920.73 ms / 1760 tokens ( 147.20 ms per token, 6.79 tokens per second) total time = 268315.40 ms / 1880 tokens graphs reused = 768 draft acceptance = 0.63548 ( 985 accepted / 1550 generated), mean len = 2.27 CLI, MTP enabled, same prompt/model: [ Prompt: 8.7 t/s | Generation: 8.5 t/s ]

items.body:
## Summary

On a gfx1151 (Strix Halo APU, RDNA3.5) system with ROCm 7.2.4, the **HIP/ROCm** backend
produces corrupted output where the **Vulkan** backend, running the **same weights, the same
build, and byte-identical flags on the same machine**, is correct on every attempt.

Measured on three architectures. Two fail on HIP, with **different severity**; one is
unaffected:

| model | `general.architecture` | topology | Vulkan | HIP/ROCm |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct `Q4_K_M` | `llama` | dense | **16/16** @30,516 · 6/6 @1,616 | **0/16** @30,516 · **0/6 @1,616** |
| Qwen3.8-27B `UD-Q8_K_XL` | `qwen35` | dense | **16/16** @29,355 | **0/16** @29,355 · 6/6 @1,349 |
| Ling-3.0-flash `IQ4_XS` | `bailingmoe3` | 512-expert MoE | **16/16** @29,275 | **16/16** @29,275 |

(`@N` = prompt tokens. Each cell is 8 requests run twice; the repeat is deliberate, because a
single 8/8 is not enough to call a backend clean.)

Backend and binary path were read from `/proc/<pid>/exe` on **every** run, not inferred from
the launcher — an earlier "Vulkan" result in this investigation turned out to be the HIP server
still answering after a boot script silently failed.

### Two severities, deliberately not merged

- **`llama` is broken outright on HIP** — at *every* depth tested, including a 1,616-token
  prompt. Output is degenerate word salad:
  `'for 4\n<|contextual background\nline keep track\nTheater in line while mind the material and context in'`
  The same model, flags and template on Vulkan is 6/6 shallow and 16/16 at 30,516 tokens, so
  this is not a configuration error.
- **`qwen35` is correct at shallow depth and fails past roughly 29k tokens** when the request
  also carries a moderately large tool array. Output stays fluent and well-formed; the model
  confidently mis-states **its own tool list**. With an array of `read_file`, `tool_00` …
  `tool_15`:

  > I don't have a `read_file` tool available in my current toolset. The tools I have access to
  > are `tool_01` through `tool_15`, which are placeholder utilities that accept a single string
  > argument. None of them are file-reading tools.

  It has read the placeholders' *descriptions* correctly while losing the entries at the **head**
  of the array. Other samples invented tool names absent from the request entirely, or ran to
  the token limit emitting `finish_reason: "length"` with empty content and no tool call.

Whether these are one defect with severity varying by model, or two, is **not established here**.

### Hypothesis, on a single data point — please treat as a lead, not a finding

The two failing models are **dense**; the one that passes is a **512-expert MoE**. Dense and
MoE matmuls take different paths (`mul_mat` vs `mul_mat_id`), which may be where to look. This
rests on **one** MoE observation and no second MoE was tested. It is offered as a starting
point, not a claim.

## Still present on current master

Reproduced on stock upstream **`b21e4de74567f5eef213765c9476a843c2e43f0d`** — `master`
re-fetched immediately before building — from a clean detached worktree with no local patches,
built for gfx1151 with ROCm 7.2.4.

The same result holds on **`3a653fea932e`** (12 days earlier). **The two SHAs agreeing is
expected rather than corroborating:** there are 7 commits between them and **none touch
`ggml/src/ggml-cuda` or `ggml/src/ggml-hip`**, so it simply means nothing has been attempted on
this code path in that window. It should not be read as an independent second confirmation.

### It is not `e79e4bf66` — please do not close this as a duplicate of that commit

`e79e4bf66` ("ggml-hip : remove -funsafe-math-optimizations", #26696) is **present in every
tested tree and does not fix this.** It is the obvious suspect and it matched on every checkable
detail:

- its message describes `-fassociative-math` reassociating FP reductions and *"can flip greedy
  argmax on **RDNA3.5** (e.g. **MTP speculative decode** diverging from the non-speculative
  baseline)"*;
- the hardware here is gfx1151, which **is** RDNA3.5;
- one of the failing workloads runs `--spec-type draft-mtp`;
- an older tree used here still carries the flag at `ggml/src/ggml-hip/CMakeLists.txt:130`,
  while every tree tested above does not.

With that flag already removed, the defect reproduces at 0/16. This is either a second,

## Overview The Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack branches on a runtime value to pick between two layouts. nvcc can't fold that, so it predicates it and then repeats the whole thing for every column of the ncols_dst loop instead of doing it once. Swapping the branch for a mask select fixes it: predicated instructions at ncols_dst=8 go from 226 to 34, and the Q4_K kernel at 16 columns from 2256 to 1648. None of the other quant types have this problem, they already unpack unconditionally (Q3_K does the same 6-bit layout with plain shifts). We see perf gains from batch size >=4 on RTX 5090 and >=5 on RTX 4090 (more details in the Performance drop down), however we do not see a gain with DGX Spark, and in fact a small regression at batch sizes 4-6, which is why the change is gated off there. The most probable reason for this can be that the memory bandwidth on DGX Spark is much lower than that of RTX 4090 or 5090, and this means even with this optimization there is no effective time to save, since in the original code the unpack was already running while the kernel waits on the weight loads and so was not adding to the total time.
Performance

## Benchmarks (RTX 5090, sm_120, CUDA 12.9, driver 620.23) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Batch size below refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Two rows per model. `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, a single forward pass of N tokens with nothing generated, which is the decode step at batch N. `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec, which also includes prefill, sampling and the draft model, and is therefore always lower. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model; only `-np` changes. The llama-server figures are total tokens over wall time at 256 tokens per request, temperature 0, across 3 runs alternating between the two builds. The request count is always a multiple of the batch size so that the final wave is not partially filled. | quant | metric | batch 1 | batch 2 | batch 4 | batch 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K_M** | decode | **-0.3%** | **+1.6%** | **+8.9%** | **+14.7%** | | | end to end | +0.4% | +1.1% | +7.4% | +10.8% | | **Q5_K_M** | decode | **+0.4%** | **+2.0%** | **+6.6%** | **+14.2%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +1.5% | +5.5% | +11.4% | | **Q6_K** * | decode | **-1.2%** | **-1.1%** | **-0.8%** | **-0.9%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +0.2% | +0.3% | +0.2% | There is no effect at batch 1, which is expected: the unpack can only be amortised once there is more than one column to share it across. ### 2. Other models Batch pinned at 4, no draft model. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Llama-3.1-8B** | decode | **+8.9%** | **+6.6%** | **-0.8%** | | | end to end | +7.4% | +5.5% | +0.3% | | **gemma-4-12B** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.8% | +6.0% | +0.1% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +8.0% | +4.2% | +0.5% | ### 3. The decode rows repeat table 2 because it is the same file at the same batch; the kernel is indifferent to the source of the batch. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **gemma-4-12B-it** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +6.2% | -0.7% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +5.5% | +0.1% | ### 4. ## Overview

disable FA GQA packing for multi-token queries

## Additional information

Speculative verify runs flash attention with neq1 > 1 (several query tokens at once). Vulkan’s GQA-packed FA path treated N <= 8 as “use GQA packing,” then overwrote N with gqa_ratio and remapped workgroups as if there were a single query token. That is only valid for single-token decode, so multi-token parallel verify disagreed with sequential FA and drifted logits (e.g. wrong-draft windows with n_win >= 4)

Related to #25618

## Validation

Setup1: Qwen3-8B Q4 + DSpark n_max=7 using vulkan on strix halo
Before Fix: Diverging output as compared to just vanilla model at same seed & zero temp
After Fix: Exact Match

Setup2: Gemma-4 Q4 + MTP n_max=4
Result: Still diverging, there are other bugs as well that I plan to handle in other PRs. See #25618

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Running MTP speculative decoding on the OpenVINO backend fails in every configuration I tried. Plain decode (same build, same model, no -md) works fine.

GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=GPU llama-cli -m gemma-4-12b-it.gguf
-md gemma-4-12b-mtp-q8.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp
-ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on -c 4096 -n 128 --temp 0 -p "test prompt"

What I tried:

1. Target and draft both on OpenVINO (command above): crashes during graph compute with a MatMul shape error, then dumps core. See first log block. Looks like the draft graph's raw hidden-state input (3840-dim, fed from the target) doesn't get a dynamic token dimension, so the post-concat MatMul shape-infers wrong.
2. Draft on CPU (-ngld 0): runs and produces correct-looking output, but logs ~505 graph-compute failures over a 128-token generation and decodes at 6.1 t/s — slower than plain decode (8.1 t/s), so speculation makes things worse.
3. Target on OPENVINO0, draft on Vulkan0 (build with both backends): aborts at ggml-backend.cpp:898 (second log block). The Gemma-4 MTP head reads the target's KV cache, which is pre-allocated in the OpenVINO buffer and can't be used from Vulkan.
4. Same as 3 with GGML_OPENVINO_STATEFUL_EXECUTION=1: throws ov::Exception from graph_rewrite.cpp:298 during compile.

This matters: on this iGPU the OpenVINO backend prefills ~6.5x faster than Vulkan (917 vs 142 t/s, pp512, Gemma-4-12B Q4_0), but Vulkan+MTP decodes ~3x faster than OpenVINO (23.5 vs 8.1 t/s). Spec-decode support is the only thing preventing the OpenVINO backend from being strictly better on Intel iGPUs.

Possibly useful data point: OpenVINO GenAI's native Gemma-4 MTP implementation works on this same GPU (measured 18.9 -> 54 t/s on Gemma-4-E2B via the optimum-intel MTP export), so the runtime handles this workload fine: the gap is in the ggml->OV translation layer.

None, appears never to have worked since the backend merged.

## Overview

#21245 already introduced the model-loading and graph-building paths for fused QKV computation. This PR further adds an opt-in `--fuse-qkv` flag to `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`: during HF-to-GGUF conversion, it concatenates the separate Q / K / V weight tensors into a single fused `attn_qkv` tensor.

- **`convert_hf_to_gguf.py`**: add the `--fuse-qkv` CLI flag. Buffer `ATTN_Q` / `ATTN_K` / `ATTN_V` per layer; once all three have arrived, concatenate them with `torch.cat` into a single fused `ATTN_QKV`. Without the flag, conversion is identical to master.
- **`gguf-py/gguf/constants.py`**: register `MODEL_TENSOR.ATTN_QKV` for every arch that already declares `ATTN_Q` + `ATTN_K` + `ATTN_V` (85 entries).
- **`src/llama-model.cpp`**: in the fused branch of `create_tensor_qkv`, if `wqkv` is found but `wqkv_b` is absent, fall back to loading the separate `wq_b` / `wk_b` / `wv_b`. `--fuse-qkv` only fuses weights, not biases, so this fallback is required.
- **`src/llama-graph.cpp`**: in the fused branch of `build_qkv`, if `wqkv_b` is absent but `wq_b` / `wk_b` / `wv_b` exist, use `ggml_concat` to concatenate the three bias segments and add them to the result of the fused matmul.

Reason for the changes in **`src/llama-model.cpp`** and **`src/llama-graph.cpp`**: on architectures with attention bias (`qwen2`, `phi2`, `starcoder2`, `stablelm`, etc.) the bias would otherwise be silently dropped, producing garbage output; after the fix the output of these archs on a `--fuse-qkv` GGUF is bit-for-bit identical to the nofuse GGUF.

**Diffstat:** 4 files, **+138 −2**.


## Test

`test-llama-archs`: all OK, 0 FAIL.

## Additional information

Following the two-step split discussed in #20628 with @am17an and @ngxson:

1. #21245 (merged) — pure refactor extracting the `build_qkv` / `create_tensor_qkv` helpers.
2. **This PR** — on top of the helpers from #21245, adds the converter-side Q/K/V weight fusion flag.

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES — used as a translation tool for translating the PR description

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

# ROCm/HIP Backend: Native gfx1031 (RX 6700 XT) Support + Flash-Attention Assert Fix

## TL;DR

On RDNA2 (gfx1031 / RX 6700 XT), the ROCm/HIP backend currently requires **two workarounds** to become usable for long-context inference: a runtime GFX-version override (masquerading as gfx1030) and a manual source patch that silences a flash-attention assert of unknown correctness impact. Once running, ROCm delivers a **~85% prefill speedup** over Vulkan at 8K context, translating to a **~23% net wall-clock win** over a full prefill+decode cycle — despite a 15–18% decode-speed deficit. This makes ROCm the clearly superior backend for this hardware *if* the build/runtime friction is resolved. This report asks for two specific fixes; a separate, still-in-progress investigation into a decode-time sampler gap (`TOP_K` unsupported on ROCm in `llama-server`) will be filed independently once sufficient data is collected.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT (gfx1031, RDNA2, Navi22) |
| CPU | Intel Core i5-11400F |
| RAM | 16GB DDR4 @ 3200 MT/s (XMP) |
| OS | Ubuntu 26.04 LTS |
| llama.cpp commit | `0a50d9909` (build 10108) |
| ROCm version | 7.1.52801-9999 |
| Compiler | clang / hipcc (`CMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang`, `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=hipcc`) |

GPU tuned via LACT (Performance level: Manual, Power Profile: Compute, power limit 182/223W, core voltage offset -90mV, VRAM 1900MHz) — same tuning applied for both backends under test, no backend-specific tuning.

## Why this matters (benchmark data)

Model: `gemma-4-12b-it-IQ4_NL.gguf` (6.24 GiB, 11.91B params). Test: `llama-bench --n-prompt 8192 --n-gen 512 --batch-size 1024 --ubatch-size 1024 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --n-gpu-layers 99 --flash-attn on`. 3 runs per backend, both with flash-attention enabled and identical batch/cache settings — the only variable changed is the backend.

| Backend | pp8192 (t/s) | tg512 (t/s) |
|---|---|---|
| ROCm (avg of 3) | 653.9 | 34.60 |
| Vulkan (avg of 3) | 354.4 | 40.92 |
| **Δ** | **+84.5%** | **-15.4%** |

Converting to wall-clock for a full 8192-prefill + 512-generate cycle:

| Backend | Prefill time | Decode time | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ROCm | 12.5s | 14.8s | **27.3s** |
| Vulkan | 23.1s | 12.5s | **35.6s** |

**ROCm wins net wall-clock by ~23%**, despite losing on raw decode throughput, because prefill dominates the cycle at this context depth. The crossover point (below which Vulkan is net-faster) is roughly ~1,760 prompt tokens — meaning ROCm is the better backend for effectively all long-context workloads on this hardware, once it can be built and run without manual intervention.

*(Decode-side deficit is currently under separate investigation — a `TOP_K` sampler op is reported unsupported on the ROCm device in `llama-server`, but this has not yet been confirmed as the cause of the `llama-bench` decode gap, since `llama-bench` explicitly excludes sampling time from its measurements. That will be reported separately once isolated.)*

## Issue 1 — gfx1031 has no working native target; requires runtime override

**Attempted:** building with `-DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1031 -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1031` directly.
**Result:** fails to run correctly on this hardware without the runtime workaround below — confirmed, not assumed.

**Current workaround:**
```bash
cmake -S ~/Projects/llama2 -B ~/Projects/llama2/build-rocm \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=hipcc \
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1030 -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1030
cmake --build ~/Projects/llama2/build-rocm -j"$(nproc)"

# at runtime, gfx1031 must masquerade as gfx1030:
HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=10.3.0 ./build-rocm/bin/llama-bench ...
```

**Ask:** native `gfx1031` target support that runs correctly without `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION`, so RX 6600/6700-series (Navi22) users don't need to build for a neighboring architecture and override the GFX version at runtime.

## Issue 2 — Flash-attention assert crash on this backend/target combo

**Location:** `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh` — `GGML_ASSERT(max_blocks_per_sm > 0);`

**Current workaround (patches source, correctness impact unknown):**
```bash
sed -i 's/GGML_ASSERT(max_blocks_per_sm > 0);/if (max_blocks_per_sm <= 0) { max_blocks_per_sm = 1; }/g' \
  ~/Projects/llama2/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh
```

## Overview

Adds the TQ1_0 ternary type (1.6875 bpw, base-3 packing — format by @compilade, thanks for TQ1_0/TQ2_0!) to the Vulkan backend. This was one of the last "TODO: implement for all backends" holes for this type, so consider it closed on Vulkan now.

What's in here:
- `block_tq1_0` struct + dequant functions, scalar and coopmat2 both
- mul_mm support in `mul_mm_funcs.glsl`
- Two new shaders: `mul_mat_vec_tq1_0.comp`, `dequant_tq1_0.comp`
- Pipeline creation + op-support wiring in `ggml-vulkan.cpp`
- Enabled TQ1_0 in test-backend-ops type lists, and added some MUL_MAT_ID cases at real MoE decode shapes (n=1, 28/128/512 experts, k=2048/4096)

Why I bothered adding those specific shapes: turns out the mat-vec shaders get `a_offset` already in block units from `get_offsets()`. My first draft divided by QUANT_K again on top of that — which is fine at offset 0 (nothing to divide, basically), but during actual mul_mat_id decode it just quietly grabs the wrong expert. No crash, no error, just wrong output. The normal test matrix never has n<16 or offset≠0 so it sailed right past. Adding these shapes would've caught it in five seconds instead of me staring at garbled output for an hour wondering what I broke. Figured it's worth keeping in the suite for whoever ports the next quant type too.

## Additional information

Ran this on my AMD Radeon 8060S (RDNA3.5 / gfx1151):

```
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT      → tq1_0 11/11 OK
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID   → tq1_0 6/6 OK
test-backend-ops test -o GET_ROWS    → tq1_0 4/4 OK
```

Also did a real run: 397B MoE, all 512 experts in TQ1_0, attention kept in Q8_0, fully resident in 96 GiB UMA on one APU. Got 10+ t/s decode, wiki PPL 5.8 — better than the best sub-2-bit quant currently out there for the same model (7.0 PPL).

# [draft-mtp] Draft acceptance collapses to 0.0 under `-np N` with multi-ubatch batches — async `t_h_nextn` device→host copy race

## Summary

Self-speculative decoding (`--spec-type draft-mtp`) silently breaks under parallel slots (`-np 4`): as soon as concurrent requests carry long prompts (decode batches spanning multiple ubatches), draft acceptance drops from a healthy **0.48–0.85** to **exactly 0.00000** on all slots, generation falls back below no-MTP speed, and consumers of the endpoint see empty `message.content` completions (`finish_reason=stop` after a handful of `reasoning_content` tokens).

The trigger is a race between the **async device→host copy of `t_h_nextn`** (the MTP draft's input hidden states) and **any later graph that reuses the `t_h_nextn` extra buffer** — the next ubatch within the same `decode()`, or the next `decode()` call under `-np N` continuous batching. When the copy loses, the MTP draft conditions on NaN `h` rows, its logits go NaN, and every draft is rejected.

Verified at [`f5b9bd39b`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/f5b9bd39b) (build 10176), HIP backend. The same binary is correct at `-np 1` and for single-ubatch batches.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| llama.cpp | [`f5b9bd39b`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/f5b9bd39b) (b10176), HIP build, `AMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151` |
| ROCm | 7.2.2 (pinned; gfx1151 native) |
| GPU | AMD Radeon 8060S (Strix Halo, gfx1151), 256 GB unified |
| Model | [unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF) `UD-Q4_K_XL` + `mmproj-F16` (`qwen35` hybrid: Gated DeltaNet + Gated Attention, embedded nextn/MTP layer) |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17 |

Server flags:

```bash
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf --jinja \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9999 -ngl all -fit off -np 4 \
  -c 1048576 -n 131072 -b 1024 -ub 256 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 \
  --load-mode dio --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 4 -rea on \
  --reasoning-format deepseek --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 --metrics
```

## Reproduction

Self-contained script (stdlib only, no client framework needed) — it fires 4 concurrent chat completions, each with a ~19k-token system prompt, and prints per-request `OK`/`EMPTY` plus finish reasons.

<details>
<summary>repro_mtp_np4.py (click to expand)</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reproduce the draft-mtp acceptance collapse under -np N concurrent load."""
import json, sys, threading, time, urllib.request

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:9999/v1/chat/completions"
N_CONC = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 4
TARGET_TOKENS = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 19000

unit = ("### Skill {i}: skill_{i} handles topic {i}. Steps: analyze, plan, "
        "execute, report. Constraints: verify outputs, cite sources.\n")
SYS = "You are an agent. Available skills:\n" + "".join(
    unit.format(i=i) for i in range(TARGET_TOKENS // 9))

def one(idx, results):
    body = {"model": "local_llm", "max_tokens": 1200, "messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYS},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"[{idx}] Say hello and list what you can help with, one line."}]}
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL, json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                 {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    t0 = time.time()
    try:
        r = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=1200))
        c = r["choices"][0]
        content = (c["message"].get("content") or "").strip()
        results.append((idx, "OK" if content else "EMPTY", c["finish_reason"],
                        r["usage"]["completion_tokens"], time.time() - t0))
    except Exception as e:
        results.append((idx, "ERROR", type(e).__name__, 0, time.time() - t0))

def round_test(round_n):
    results = []
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=one, args=(i, results)) for i in range(N_CONC)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    empty = sum(1 for r in results if r[1] != "OK")
    for r in results:
        print(f"  round {round_n} req{r[0]}: {r[1]:5s} finish={r[2]:6s} ct={r[3]:5d} {r[4]:7.1f}s")
    print(f"  round {round_n}: empty {empty}/{N_CONC}")
    return empty

if __name__ == "__main__":
    total = sum(round_test(n + 1) for n in range(2))
    print(f"TOTAL empty: {total}/{2 * N_CONC}")
```

</details>

### Expected output on an affected build

Server log (`--metrics`, per slot, at task end):

```
slot print_timing: id 0 | draft acceptance = 0.00000 (    0 accepted /   4786 generated), mean len = 1.00
slot print_timing: id 1 | draft acceptance = 0.00000 (    0 accepted /   4786 generated), mean len = 1.00
slot print_timing: id 2 | draft acceptance = 0.00000 (    0 accepted /   4786 generated), mean len = 1.00
slot print_timing: id 3 | draft acceptance = 0.00000 (    0 accepted /   4786 generated), mean len = 1.00
```

The same server, **sequential** single request on a cold slot:

```
slot print_timing: id 3 | draft acceptance = 0.57865 (  206 accepted /   356 generated), mean len = 3.31
```

Client side, affected requests return `finish_reason=stop` with empty content after a few reasoning tokens, or run away in reasoning until the token cap — both surface as "empty completion" to an agent/chat client.

### What does *not* trigger it

- `-np 4` with short prompts (single-ubatch batches): 0/12 failures over 3 rounds
- Long prompts processed **sequentially** (one slot active): healthy acceptance
- Warm prefix cache (prefill mostly cached): healthy
- `-np 1` with MTP: always healthy

→ the failure requires **concurrent** requests producing decode calls whose batches split across ubatches (long prompts), under multi-slot continuous batching.

Instrumentation adds two probes (patch inlined at the end of this section):

1. In `llama_context::decode()`'s per-ubatch `t_h_nextn` extraction: after the async copy, `ggml_backend_sched_synchronize()` then compare the **device tensor** contents (via synchronou

## Overview

DFlash2 adds two more modules compared to DFlash, grouped dynamic depthwise convolution and candidate selector. 

The formula is for reference. `out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c]`. `base` is the static kernel, `δ` is the dynamic part predicted from the input.`x` is divided into groups `g(c)` and `δ` is shared across a group. Another one is `edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c]`. `A`/`B` are the codebooks for the predecessor and the candidate. This position's hidden is projected by `project(h)`to the same rank to multiply `A`. And `unary[c]` is the draft's own score for `c`.  

DFlash2 is enabled when the checkpoint is DFlash2; no need to use extra flag.

We evaled `Qwen3.8-27B` at `Q4_K_M`on Apple M5 Pro 64 GB. And the test data is first 8 problems of GSM8K.
Concurrency is set to 1 and temperature is 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20. We use default `xhigh` reasoning and set
2,048 maximum new tokens.

| Method | Draft quant | Block | Decode TPS | Decode speedup | Acceptance | Normal stops |
|--------|------|--:|------:|------:|-----:|---|
| Autoregressive | — | — | 10.42 | 1.00× | — | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | BF16 | 8 | 19.31 | 1.85× | 4.92 | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | Q8_0 | 8 | 18.43 | 1.77× | 5.08 | 8/8 |
